test_set: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner. (tests exclamation, humour)
2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late. (anger tell, numbers; say it to someone other than you)
3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job. (praise, feeling said or shown; keep the cousin's gender open)
4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it. (humour, a polite no; say it to someone other than you)
5. In front of the family, someone shows that they had a fact wrong. (sorry, anger)
6. Someone they love is leaving, and they say goodbye on a railway platform. (love, feeling)
7. Someone thanks them for something they did. (thanks)
8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing. (humour, habits not character; harmless rumour, rule 22 safe; say it to someone other than you)
9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house. (worry, where their words come from)
10. Someone asks them how they are. (feeling, the C10 dodges)
11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table. (comfort, kindness; say it to someone other than you)
12. A phone call brings good news. (joy, exclamation)

HOW TO RUN: each of the eleven reacts in one bubble of at most 10 words (Hinglish, then Hindi and English); all rules hold (rule 3 list in matrix.md 2.13, numbers only for Papa and Tinku plus marked exceptions, rule 66 on every line to or from you, British spelling, no dashes). Shuffle the 132 lines untagged; a reader who did not write them sorts by speaker using only the target cards. Pass: each person sorted right at least 10 of 12 times and no pair confused more than twice; any pair confused 3 or more times is fixed before any panel is written. Repeat in Hindi and English.

problems.name: All eleven files (checker summary and one gap in rule 66's flag list)
problems.line: Every sample, typing sample and test line in nani, mummy, papa, mama-ji, tinku, mausi, mausa-ji, masterji, captain-sahab, mami and you.json: 1,600 lines in three languages, 1,951 bubbles
problems.problem: What came back clean: no religious word or exclamation, no caste word, no brand, no em or en dash anywhere in the files, and no American spelling (the only hits were 'fall', which means Nani's fall). No spoken bubble goes over 10 counted words. Rule 66's checks flagged 153 player lines; I read every one and they are all fine, apart from the lines listed below. One gap in the rule itself: the three flags miss commands built from a participle plus रहो or रहना (खाते रहो to a man, खाती रहो to a woman). Mama ji's own never list already bans बैठे रहो and खड़े रहो for this reason. The other two intermediate files were skipped: _papa_return.json is identical to papa.json, and _mummy_base.json has no lines. The baseline files hold the old lines, not the rewrites.
problems.fix: Add a fourth flag to rule 66: a word ending in -ते, -ती or -तीं just before रहो, रहना, रहिए or रहें. The script already checks for it. The script is /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/voice/check/voice_check.py (run it with python3 -I). It writes report.txt and report.json next to itself. dump_lines.py in the same folder prints one character's lines for a read-through.

problems.name: Mama ji
problems.line: test[9], to you: 'फ़ुल फ़िट! अम्मा ने दवाई ली? दीदी? पक्का?' | 'Full fit! Amma ne dawai li? Didi? Pakka?' | 'Fighting fit! Has Amma had her medicines? Didi? Sure?'
problems.problem: Rules 8 and 66. In a bubble spoken to the player, 'Didi?' standing on its own reads as Mama ji calling the player Didi, which gives the player a gender. He means Mummy, but the reader cannot tell. The checker flags this as a lone kin word.
problems.fix: 'फ़ुल फ़िट! अम्मा ने दवाई ली? दीदी कैसी हैं? पक्का?' | 'Full fit! Amma ne dawai li? Didi kaisi hain? Pakka?' | 'Fighting fit! Has Amma had her medicines? How's Didi? Sure?' (कैसी हैं agrees with Didi; 8 counted words)

problems.name: Nani
problems.line: test[0], to the whole table: 'कोई टॉर्च लाए। बाक़ी खाते रहो।' | 'Koi torch laaye. Baaki khaate raho.'
problems.problem: Rule 66 (the gap above). खाते रहो agrees with its listeners, as masculine or mixed plural. The player is at the table, and the same shape said to the player alone would mark a gender. Mama ji's file bans this shape. Today's three flags miss it.
problems.fix: 'कोई टॉर्च लाए। बाक़ी सब खाओ।' | 'Koi torch laaye. Baaki sab khao.' | 'Someone fetch a torch. The rest, eat.'

problems.name: Mama ji
problems.line: Catchphrase 'Pakka?' | 'पक्का?' | 'Sure?' (it ends every worry stack), and the voice.never list
problems.problem: Rule 22: the household never doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand. Every other file has that guard in its never list. Mama ji's file bans only dowry and ritual words. His reflex 'Pakka?' is the very word Mausi's never list names as doubt ('sach mein?', 'pakka?'). Said after a report, it would read as disbelief.
problems.fix: Add to his never list: 'Any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22); never "Pakka?" or any question back after one.' Give him a believe-first line, for example 'मैं आ रहा हूँ। अभी।' | 'Main aa raha hoon. Abhi.' | 'I'm coming. Now.' (his own male form; the line says nothing about the player).

problems.line: sample[4], to you: 'बड़ी का घुटना? नीचे की बर्थ।' | 'Badi ka ghutna? Neeche ki berth.'
problems.problem: Clarity. Her pet name 'Badi' is opaque to the player-reader, and the English says 'Mausi's knee'. To you she already says 'तुम्हारी मम्मी' in sample[17]. Mausi's 'छोटी' for Mummy in lines to you (sample[4], sample[6], typing[0]) has the same problem, more mildly.
problems.fix: 'तुम्हारी मौसी का घुटना? नीचे की बर्थ।' | 'Tumhari Mausi ka ghutna? Neeche ki berth.' For Mausi, use 'तुम्हारी मम्मी' the first time she names Mummy to you in a chapter, then 'छोटी'.

problems.name: Mausi
problems.line: sample[3], to Papa and Mausa ji: 'चलो, चलो, चलो! बड़े वाले ऊपर! जल्दी!' | 'Chalo, chalo, chalo!'
problems.problem: Politeness check. Her own file says she uses आप to Papa, but this hurry-up goes to him in the तुम form. As a bustling particle to a group it is said, but a Hindi-first reader may hear it as a step down for a jija.
problems.fix: 'चलिए, चलिए, चलिए! बड़े वाले ऊपर! जल्दी!' | 'Chaliye, chaliye, chaliye!' (keeps her triple). Or keep चलो and have a Hindi-first reader sign it off.

problems.name: Nani
problems.line: sample[14], to the doctor: 'मुझसे पूछिए। बीमार। बहरी नहीं।' | 'Mujhse poochhiye. Beemar. Behri nahin.'
problems.problem: Naturalness. 'बीमार।' on its own reads as a stray word. The saying is 'ill, not deaf' said as one thought.
problems.fix: 'मुझसे पूछिए। बीमार हूँ, बहरी नहीं।' | 'Mujhse poochhiye. Beemar hoon, behri nahin.' (her own female form, said to the doctor, so rule 66 does not apply)

problems.name: Nani
problems.line: sample[3]: 'रात भर। डॉक्टर की सलाह। मेरी हाँ।' | 'Raat bhar. Doctor ki salaah. Meri haan.'
problems.problem: Naturalness. 'मेरी हाँ' is not an everyday phrase for 'my say-so'.
problems.fix: 'रात भर। डॉक्टर की सलाह। और मेरी मर्ज़ी।' | 'Raat bhar. Doctor ki salaah. Aur meri marzi.'

problems.name: Mausa ji
problems.line: sample[4], to you at dawn: 'नींद हुई?' | 'Neend hui?'
problems.problem: Naturalness. The everyday question is whether sleep came, not whether sleep happened.
problems.fix: 'नींद आई?' | 'Neend aayi?' (आई agrees with नींद, so rule 66 stays clean)

problems.name: Mausa ji
problems.line: sample[3]: 'स्विच बंद। तब हाथ।' and sample[15]: 'अंदर करो।' and sample[9]: 'हम्म। काम था।'
problems.problem: Naturalness (low). 'तब हाथ।' is cryptic. Money is 'put away' with रखो, not करो. 'काम था।' reads as 'there was work' rather than 'just the job'.
problems.fix: 'स्विच बंद। तब हाथ लगाना।' (an infinitive command, no gender) | 'अंदर रखो।' | 'हम्म। काम ही था।' with matching Hinglish: 'Switch band. Tab haath lagaana.' | 'Andar rakho.' | 'Hmm. Kaam hi tha.'

problems.name: Masterji
problems.line: test[5], goodbye, possibly to you: 'जाओ। कपड़ा दूर जाए, सिलाई यहीं की रहती है।' | 'Jao. Kapda door jaaye, silai yahin ki rehti hai.'
problems.problem: Naturalness. 'कपड़ा दूर जाए' reads as a wish ('may the cloth go far') rather than 'cloth travels far'.
problems.fix: 'जाओ। कपड़ा कहीं भी जाए, सिलाई यहीं की रहती है।' | 'Jao. Kapda kahin bhi jaaye, silai yahin ki rehti hai.' (10 words, at the cap; rule 66 clean)

problems.name: Mummy
problems.line: sample[12], to a stranger needing a fuse: 'ले जाइए, जी। क्रेडिट बुक में लिख दिया, आराम से।'
problems.problem: Naturalness in Hindi mode. A shopkeeper writes it in the khaata or as udhaar, not in a 'क्रेडिट बुक'. The comma inside 'ले जाइए, जी' is also off.
problems.fix: 'ले जाइए जी। खाते में लिख दिया, आराम से।' (Hinglish can keep 'Le jaiye ji. Credit book mein likh diya, aaram se.')

problems.name: Mummy
problems.line: test[2], to the cousin: 'हाँ जी, बोलिए। नौकरी? लेटर भेजो, काउंटर पर लगाऊँगी।'
problems.problem: The register switches inside one line, from आप (बोलिए) to तुम (भेजो), with the same listener. That works only if the reader sees the shop greeting drop once she knows the voice.
problems.fix: If the switch is not meant: 'लेटर भेजिए' | 'Letter bhejiye'. If it is meant, add the moment of recognition first, as her voice note does with 'अच्छा तुम'.

problems.name: Mami
problems.line: sample[14], to Nani: 'मम्मी जी, आपकी चाय हो गई? तो मेहमान।' | 'Toh mehmaan.'
problems.problem: Naturalness. 'तो मेहमान' ('so, guests') does not read as 'then the guests'.
problems.fix: 'मम्मी जी, आपकी चाय हो गई? उसके बाद मेहमान।' | 'Uske baad mehmaan.' (avoids 'phir', which goes with the player's 'Pehle')

problems.name: Mami
problems.line: test[0], to you: 'इश्श। बत्ती, गई। तुम्हारे मामा जी का खाना: चालू।' (and her other Hindi status pairs, such as 'टेंट, हो गया')
problems.problem: Naturalness (low). A comma between a Hindi subject and its verb looks like a typing slip, not a status line. In the same bubble she already uses a colon ('खाना: चालू').
problems.fix: Use her colon in Hindi status pairs: 'इश्श। बत्ती: गई। तुम्हारे मामा जी का खाना: चालू।', 'टेंट: हो गया।'

problems.name: Captain sahab
problems.line: Hindi mode: sample[14] 'वेल प्लेड।', sample[15] and [16] 'वेल फ़ील्डेड, ...', sample[17] and test[4] 'नेक्स्ट बॉल।', sample[18] 'नेक्स्ट बॉल, भाभी जी।', test[1] 'टाइम्ड आउट।', test[2] 'वेल प्लेड।', test[10] 'नेक्स्ट बॉल।'
problems.problem: Rule 65 (Hindi written fresh in everyday spoken words). Whole English umpire phrases written in Devanagari are hard for a Hindi-first reader. 'Timed out' is obscure even in English. Out, no ball, catch and not out are everyday Hindi cricket words and can stay.
problems.fix: In Hindi mode only: 'अगली गेंद' for नेक्स्ट बॉल, 'बढ़िया फ़ील्डिंग, लाइनमैन साहब।' for वेल फ़ील्डेड, 'बढ़िया पारी।' for वेल प्लेड (पारी is feminine and बढ़िया never changes, so no gender), and 'टाइम आउट। उस कैच की तरह।' for टाइम्ड आउट. Hinglish keeps the English calls.

problems.name: Captain sahab
problems.line: test[0], to the table: 'रुको। लाइनमैन साहब, आपकी बैटिंग।' and the stock phrase in voice.uses: 'सबूत नहीं, तो उँगली नहीं।' | 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.'
problems.problem: (a) Politeness: 'रुको' goes to a table that can include Nani, who is 80 and older than him. (b) Rule 22: 'No proof, no finger' is fine for a sweet-shop rumour (test[7]). As a stock phrase it is the shape of doubt, and it must never come near a report of harassment or a dowry demand. His never list bans doubt but does not fence this phrase off.
problems.fix: (a) 'रुकिए।' | 'Rukiye.' when an elder is at the table. (b) Add to his never list: 'सबूत नहीं, तो उँगली नहीं' and any call for proof, never in a chapter or beat that holds a hard topic.

problems.name: Mama ji
problems.line: typing to Tinku: 'सो प्राउड 🤗'; typing to Mummy: 'मिस यू ऑल 🤗'
problems.problem: Naturalness in Hindi mode (low). Someone who types in Devanagari rarely spells out English phrases. A Hindi-first reader would expect Hindi words here.
problems.fix: 'बहुत गर्व है 🤗' and 'सबकी याद आती है 🤗' (both gender-free). Hinglish keeps 'so proud' and 'miss you all'.

problems.name: Mama ji and Papa
problems.line: Mama ji sample[14]: 'अगले साल की टिकट भी बुक? / और हाँ, मेरी भी' against Papa sample[5]: 'कल की गाड़ी का टिकट' and test[6]: 'वापसी का टिकट'
problems.problem: Consistency (low). The two use different genders for टिकट. Both are heard in real speech (standard masculine, regional feminine), but readers may see it as a slip.
problems.fix: Keep it only if it is meant as a voice mark (Papa standard, Mama ji colloquial), and say so in both files. Otherwise use 'अगले साल का टिकट भी बुक? / और हाँ, मेरा भी'.

notes.name: Cast-wide
problems: VERDICT. Most of the eleven now sound like real people, and you can tell them apart by how their lines are shaped. The number problem is mostly fixed: Mummy has no prices, Nani no head-counts, Masterji no inches, Mami no ordinals. All eleven exclamations are free of religion, and no two people share one. What still sounds written rather than heard comes from four habits across the cast. These are points 1 to 4 below. The persons' notes give exact replacement lines.

1. COMMON FILLERS ARE BANNED. The one-owner table took the most common words of spoken Hindi away from nearly everyone. arre is Captain sahab's only; chalo and suno are Mausi's; dekho is Masterji's; bas is Nani's; theek is Mausa ji's; achha and pakka are Mama ji's; haan ji is Mummy's; sorry is Mausi's; thank you is Mami's; fikr is Masterji's. The realism notes (1.3) say these fillers 'belong to everyone' and mark no region, religion or gender. Without them a house sounds sterile, and that sterile sound is why Ravi would call lines translated. FIX: let owners keep phrases, not fillers. Captain sahab keeps 'Arre waah.', Mausa ji keeps a one-word 'Theek.', Nani keeps 'Bas.' as her closer and Mausi keeps 'Suno, suno, suno!'. Everyone may say arre, achha, haan, chalo, dekho, suno, bas and theek hai in the middle of a line. The blind sort already works by line shape, so it does not need these bans.

2. ONLY MUMMY MAY USE AN ENGLISH VERB WITH kar OR ho. This is the most common Hinglish pattern in India. A city pump salesman (Mama ji), a city billing manager (Mami), a 21-year-old student (Tinku) and a player aged 22 to 30 all say 'miss kiya', 'call karo' and 'adjust karo' every day. The realism notes give Tinku 'English clauses with Hindi tags', and the pass took those out too. FIX: let everyone under about 50 use it. Mark Mummy out by what she turns into a shop verb: home things in counter English ('ye cup return karo', 'MCB check karo').

3. SORRY AND THANKS ARE STILL CODED. The reviews said elders swap them for a deed. The pass swapped them for trade words instead: 'Darj hai', 'Ye mere hisaab mein', 'Iska bill nahin', 'Mera item tha', 'Tick', 'Mera wicket', 'Run tumhara', 'Well fielded', 'Ab ye tumhari chai wali barsaat', 'Chai piyo'. Eight of eleven still use a code; only Mausi, Mama ji and You say it plainly. It is still one writer's trick, just in nine trades. Real north Indian elders thank the young in other ways: a blessing that names no god ('Khush raho', 'Jeete raho'), a brush-off ('Arre, isme kya'), or 'Shabaash'. Young people say 'sorry' and 'thank you' in English. FIX: give Nani 'Khush raho' and Masterji 'Jeete raho'; the owner and the Hindi-first readers should confirm that these pass rule 3. Give Tinku and You a plain English sorry and thank-you. Let each trade code appear at most once a chapter.

4. NOBODY CONGRATULATES. In test moment 3 (a cousin's first job), no one says 'Badhai ho' or 'Congratulations', which is the most natural line there is. Mama ji's file bans 'Badhaai ho' because it is a film title. Rule 3 only bans brands, famous people, ritual and symbols on screen, not everyday phrases, and this one is centuries older than the film. FIX (owner question): if it is allowed, give 'Badhai ho!' to Mummy and 'Congratulations.' to Mami. Leave 'Mubarak ho' unused, so the congratulation leans to no one community.

5. RULE 22 RISK. Two catchphrases demand proof: Captain sahab's 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' and Mami's 'Status, not known. Is it in writing?'. Both are fine about a sweet-shop rumour. In a game with harassment and dowry reports, though, either one sits one screenshot away from 'the family wants proof' (anti-persona A2), and Farida would read it that way. FIX: never use either line in a chapter that holds a report twin. Add a build flag for proof words (saboot, likhit, writing, proof) placed near a report beat.

6. SHARED BITS BREAK THE VOICE TEST. Nani ('Chai mein cheeni? Ya cheeni mein chai?') and Papa ('Is cheeni mein chai bhi hai.') tell the same sugar joke. Papa ('Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon') and Mausa ji (who stands on the platform till the last coach) share the same goodbye. In moment 2, five people reach for cold food; in moment 11, four say 'only water'. The test set is fine, but any two of these in one panel will clash. Fixes are in Papa's and Mausa ji's notes.

7. EXCLAMATIONS BY REGION. None is religious. Two lean to one region: Mausi's 'Haaye', spelled the way Punjabi aunties are spelled in films (fix in her note), and Mami's Bengali 'Ish', which is on purpose and right if kept to dismay. Tinku's 'oye' is Delhi and Punjab street talk, but fine kept rare. 'Baap re' sounds like Mumbai and Bihar, but it is used across the Hindi belt, and Farida will hear her own city in it. 'Gazab' sounds like UP, which suits a junction town.

8. URDU-ROOTED WORDS SIT ON ONE MAN. Only Masterji may say fikr, farq, waqt, zaroor and khair, and the other files ban them. That turns everyday Hindustani into the tailor's badge, and tailoring is the trade films most often show as Muslim. Players will guess a community the file never gives him. FIX: let two or three others use fikr, waqt and zaroor normally, so these words belong to the town, not to him.

9. TOO MANY LINES WITH NO VERB. Seven of eleven still speak in short, clipped lines, and five of them mostly leave out the verb or 'hai' (Nani, Mummy, Mausa ji, Captain sahab, Mami). Each shape is now different, which is real progress. Together, though, they make a house that talks in telegrams: spoken Hindi drops 'hai' some of the time, not in every line from five people. FIX: give Nani, Mummy and Mami their 'hai' or 'hoon' in comfort and love lines, and keep the bare shapes for orders and lists.

10. ENGLISH MODE SOUNDS TRANSLATED. Shruti and Mr Natarajan, the English-mode players, will hear many lines as word-for-word translation: 'Mountain out of a mustard seed', 'Milk is milk, water is water', 'Drop by drop, the pot fills', 'Tinku the cloth, me a new glass, you a biscuit', 'everyone comes!!', 'This is the monsoon of your tea now', 'Put that on my account', 'Thank-yous are for the counter', 'In the monsoon even clocks swell', 'Mind you,' at the start of nearly every Masterji line, 'Ugh.', 'Oh, nice.', 'Lovely.' and 'That's the limit!'. Fixes are in each person's note.

11. HINDI MODE IS HARD FOR LOW-ENGLISH READERS. Sunita and Meena, who read little English, get Captain sahab's calls as English written in Devanagari: टाइम्ड आउट, डेड बॉल, रिटायर्ड हर्ट, वेल फ़ील्डेड. Lane cricket fans know 'out', 'not out', 'no ball' and 'front foot'; few know the other four. Mami's status words with commas between them read as an English list. Fixes are in their notes.

notes.name: Nani
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Baap re' said low; 'Dandi mat maarna'; 'Raai ka pahaad'; 'Mujhse poochhiye. Beemar. Behri nahin.'; 'Giri nahin. Baith gayi. Zor se.'; the sugar tease; 'Bori upar. Chappal upar. Bachche andar.'; 'Bas. Apni sunao.'; 'Badi' and 'Chhote'; her voice typing; and 'Haan, subah ho gayi.' under Papa's flower. Sunita and Ravi will know this grandmother.

TELEGRAM COMFORT. With no verb and no 'hai', her comfort reads like a telegram: 'Main yahin. Kahin nahin.', 'Raat bhar. Doctor ki salaah. Meri haan.', 'Paani. Ghee nahin.'. A real 80-year-old rambles more than anyone else in the house. FIX: keep the fragments for orders, but give comfort and asides their verb. 'Main yahin hoon. Kahin nahin jaa rahi.' | 'मैं यहीं हूँ। कहीं नहीं जा रही।' | 'I'm right here. Not going anywhere.' Then 'Paani hi toh hai. Ghee nahin.' | 'पानी ही तो है। घी नहीं।' | 'It's only water. Not ghee.' Then 'Doctor ki salaah thi. Maine haan kar di.' | 'डॉक्टर की सलाह थी। मैंने हाँ कर दी।' | 'Doctor's advice. I said yes.' All three are about Nani, so rule 66 is untouched.

COINED SAYINGS. Two lines break her own rule that every saying is a real one. Nobody praises with 'Poora taul.', and 'Tumhara taraazu sachcha.' is made up too. FIX: praise with the real idiom: 'Kaam khara utra.' | 'काम खरा उतरा।' | 'Up to the mark.' (it agrees with काम, so it gives you no gender). Concede plainly: 'Scorer sahi. Main galat. Chai piyo.' | 'स्कोरर सही। मैं ग़लत। चाय पियो।' | 'The scorer's right. I was wrong. Drink your tea.' Use the fixed phrase people actually say: 'Tol-mol ke bolo.' | 'तोल-मोल के बोलो।' | 'Weigh your words.'

WARMTH LOST. She has no pet name and no blessing, and her platform goodbye is an order: 'Chhote. Jhuko. Ab jaao.'. A real Nani blesses and asks for a call. FIX for the goodbye, with her palm on his head as drawn: 'Khush raho. Pahunchkar phone karna.' | 'ख़ुश रहो। पहुँचकर फ़ोन करना।' | 'Be happy. Ring when you get there.' It names no god and the command marks no gender; the owner should confirm rule 3. Moment 3 becomes 'Khush raho. Mithai tumhari taraf se.' | 'ख़ुश रहो। मिठाई तुम्हारी तरफ़ से।' | 'Bless you. The sweets are on you.' In English mode, 'Bless you' suggests God, so use 'Well done. The sweets are on you.'

'SCORER' AS A LABEL. Nani says 'Scorer' to Tinku in every mode. An 80-year-old Hindi-only grocer using an English job word for her granddaughter every time is a gimmick, not a tease. FIX: say 'Tinku' in plain lines, and 'Scorer' only when the scorebook proves her right (moment 5).

ENGLISH MODE. Replace word-for-word sayings with the English ones people know. 'Mountain out of a mustard seed.' becomes 'Mountain out of a molehill.' 'Drop by drop, the pot fills.' becomes 'Little drops make an ocean.', the English saying Indian schoolchildren learn. 'Milk is milk, water is water. Tell me.' becomes 'The plain truth. No water in it. Tell me.' 'Well I never.' for 'Baap re' sounds like an English grandmother. Either keep it, or keep 'Baap re.' in English mode too, the way Mami keeps 'Ish.'.

notes.name: Mummy
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Haan ji, boliye' even to her own children; 'Had hai!'; 'Main hi hoon. Boliye, delivery kab?'; 'Bhindi itni mehngi? Kal se sabzi main laaungi.'; her cross politeness ('Tinku ji, nau baj gaye. Aap kahaan hain?', 'Chhote ji, aap hi chala lijiye. Chaabi ye rahi.'); the credit book opened in flood week; and 'Band? Unka shutter aaj bhi utha.'. Ravi and Sunita have bought from this woman.

COINED SORRY. 'Ye mere hisaab mein.' (Put that on my account) is made up, and listeners will ask what is in whose account. The real shop idiom is 'mere khaate mein daal do'. FIX: 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid, mere khaate mein daaliye.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद, मेरे खाते में डालिए।' | 'Masterji, last night's stubbornness: put it down to me.'

COLD COMFORT. At 2 am in the flood her comfort is only a schedule: 'Paani kal, maal parson, shutter Shanivaar.'. A mother adds one plain care line. FIX, as a second bubble: 'Ab let jao. Baaki subah.' | 'अब लेट जाओ। बाक़ी सुबह।' | 'Lie down now. The rest in the morning.' It is a command, so no gender, and it is not Mausa ji's 'So jao'.
NO CONGRATULATION. Moment 3 has none (see cast-wide 4). FIX, if the owner allows it: 'Haan ji, boliye. Naukri? Badhai ho!' and then 'Letter bhejo, counter pe lagaungi.'

TRADER STEREOTYPE. 'Calendar muft. Keel ka bill alag.' and 'Udhaar? Kal.' are both the stingy-shopkeeper joke that the realism notes and the India review warn against. Ravi's cousins would forward the calendar line as exactly that. FIX: cut the calendar joke. Keep 'Udhaar? Kal.' only in a chapter that also shows her credit book open.

ENGLISH MODE. 'That's the limit!' is not how Indian English puts it; Indian English says 'This is too much!'. Moment 11, 'Tinku the cloth, me a new glass, you a biscuit.', becomes 'Tinku, cloth. I'll get a glass. You, a biscuit.'

notes.name: Papa
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). His whole-sentence, announcement-style Hindi; 'Reached?'; the 6:35 good-morning flower; 'Kripya dhyan dein. Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.' (every player will laugh); 'Batti das baje bujhegi.'; 'Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.'; 'The dal is on the stove.'; 'Sab gaadiyan time par hain. Matlab main bhi.'. The Tamil whisper count is correct spoken Tamil (naalu, anju, aaru). Mr Natarajan will like that it is a habit, not a joke.

MINUTES INSTEAD OF FEELINGS. In three places his minutes still make him a robot. Nobody says '120 minute der se'; railway people say 'do ghante'. His thanks is '5:52 par chai seedhi par thi. Darj hai.', and his good news is 'Khabar 11:52 par aayi. Darj kar li.'. FIX: 'Tum do ghante der se aaye. Khana thanda hai. Thanda.' For thanks, praise the timing: 'Mummy ji, chai bilkul time par thi.' | 'मम्मी जी, चाय बिल्कुल टाइम पर थी।' | 'Mummy ji, the tea was right on time.' For good news: 'Kamaal hai. Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.' | 'कमाल है। मम्मी जी को अभी बताता हूँ।' | 'Remarkable. I'll tell Mummy ji right away.'

'DARJ HAI' AS THANKS. 'Darj hai.' is a register-book word. To a Hindi-first ear it sounds like an office, not a man thanking his mother-in-law. FIX: keep it as his reply to a fact ('Noted.' in his typing is perfect), never as a thank-you to family.

ODD ANNOUNCEMENT. In moment 11, 'Ab kapda aayega.' (The cloth comes next) is his announcement habit gone strange. FIX: 'Koi baat nahin. Gilaas seedha karo. Kapda main laata hoon.' | 'कोई बात नहीं। गिलास सीधा करो। कपड़ा मैं लाता हूँ।' | 'Never mind. Stand the glass up. I'll get a cloth.'

SUGAR JOKE COLLISION. His sugar joke is the same as Nani's (cast-wide 6). FIX, in his own announcement frame: 'Kripya dhyan dein. Ye chai nahin, sharbat hai.' | 'कृपया ध्यान दें। ये चाय नहीं, शरबत है।' | 'Attention, please. This is not tea. It is sherbet.'

'PITAJI'. 'Mere pitaji' is said mostly in Hindu and Sikh homes. The lean is light, like the reason 'Mataji' was struck. FIX: the Hindi-first and Urdu-speaking readers should confirm it. If they flag it, he can say 'Mere father guard the' only in English mode and keep 'pitaji' in Hindi.

notes.name: Mama ji
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Pakka?'; 'Oho!'; 'Boss' for his wife; 'Ghar mein sab theek? Maa ji ka ghutna?' to every vendor; 'Aa gaye, bhai? Ghar mein sab theek? Achha. Tent. Abhi.'; 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega'; and texts like 'Didi!!', 'ok ok call me', 'DISTRICT LEVEL!! 🎉🎉'. Ravi has this uncle.

'AUR HAAN' EVERYWHERE. 'aur haan,' ends 8 of his 12 test lines. A trailing comma on nearly every bubble is a gimmick, and on a phone it looks as if the bubble was cut off. FIX: one 'aur haan' a scene. Other runs end on 'Pakka?' or a full stop.

LOVE LINE. His love line is built around the ban on English verb + kar, and 'Amma, I missed you. Roz.' reads as a translation of 'every day'. FIX: 'Amma, aapko roz miss kiya.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना एक दिन भी मन नहीं लगा।' | 'Amma, I missed you every single day.' This depends on cast-wide 2.

RUMOUR LINE. In moment 8, 'Mithai wale bhai ki maa ji theek? Pakka?' jumps straight to the shopkeeper's mother. It reads as the people-first trick, not a reaction. FIX: 'Oho. Band? Mithai wale bhai theek toh hain? Pakka?' | 'ओहो। बंद? मिठाई वाले भाई ठीक तो हैं? पक्का?' | 'Oho. Closing? Is the sweet-shop man all right? Sure?'
TYPED ENGLISH. 'everyone comes!!' is a word-for-word 'sab aayein'. FIX: 'everyone must come!!'

'FULL' OVERUSED. 'full' is real city slang, but it now shows up in his sorry ('full kasoor mera'), his health ('full fit') and his tea ('chai full meethi'). Together with 'extra', that turns into the slangy-uncle gimmick. FIX: 'full' in at most two lines a chapter. The other times say 'poora' ('Poora kasoor mera, Didi.').

notes.name: Tinku
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Gazab!'; the 'haan?' tag; 'Batti gul, khel band.' / 'Bad light stops play.'; '80, not out, Nani.' (Indians say this at birthdays, so it will land); 'Ji nahin, Mami.'; 'Papa aaj 4 baar tok chuke. Record.'; polite Devanagari to Nani; and texts like 'oye / mama ji called u again', 'mausi ka voice note / 2x pe bhi khatam nahi', 'abhi sirf tumhe bataya / gazabbb'.

EVERY FEELING IS CRICKET. Sorry is 'Mera wicket', thanks is 'Run tumhara', love is 'not out', a goodbye is 'Innings abhi baaki', and a job is 'Kya debut!'. Scoring is how she sees things, but a 21-year-old says feelings plainly and in English. With Captain sahab, cricket talk is their bond; with everyone else it is a gimmick. FIX: keep 'Mera wicket' and 'Run aapka' for Captain sahab. Elsewhere, sorry is 'Sorry, meri galti. 14 nahin, 15.' | 'सॉरी, मेरी ग़लती। चौदह नहीं, पंद्रह।' | 'Sorry, my mistake. Fifteen, not fourteen.' Mausi keeps her tripled sorry with food held out, so the two still sort apart. Thanks to you is 'Thank you. Kal raat ki dawai tumne sambhali.' | 'थैंक यू। कल रात की दवाई तुमने सँभाली।' | 'Thanks. You handled last night's medicines.' The ने past agrees with दवाई, so it gives you no gender.

COLD CONGRATULATION. In moment 3, 'Kya debut! Seedhe kitaab mein.' is cold for a cousin's first job. Every 21-year-old says the party line. FIX: 'Gazab! Party kab hai?' | 'ग़ज़ब! पार्टी कब है?' | 'Brilliant! When's the party?'

NO ENGLISH AT HOME. She has no whole English clause at home and no English verb + kar, yet the realism notes give her 'English clauses with Hindi tags'. A commerce student with no English in her speech is the least real thing about her. FIX: allow short English clauses ('Mama ji, seriously? Phir se?', 'Relax karo, Mausi.') while keeping slang words like 'literally' and 'vibe' out, as the caricature notes ask.

ADDRESS TO YOU. 'oye' is Delhi and Punjab street talk. It is real among friends but kept rare, which is right. 'yaar' marks no gender and young women everywhere say it. FIX: it would be a more everyday word for her to use to you; the owner and readers can clear it under rules 8 and 66.

notes.name: Mausi
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). The most alive voice in the pass: 'Bahut yaad aayi'; 'Rishta main laayi thi. Berth bhi main laaun?'; 'Kaisi hoon? Batati hoon! Ghutna dukhta hai, dil nahin!'; 'Chehre pe thakaan! Kuch khaya bhi?'; 'Na, na, na! Band? Toh meri class ka inaam?'; 'Late mark!'; 'Ekdum first class!'; the real children's riddle 'ek thaal moti se bhara'; her '....' typing with 😊; 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya??'. Sunita knows her.

TOO MANY TRIPLES. A tripled word opens 8 of her 12 test lines and nearly every sample: suno, chalo, na, sorry, aao, Munna, Aji, Bhabhi, each three times. Real Hindi doubles ('chalo chalo', 'na na', 'suno suno'), and saves the triple for a peak. FIX: double by default, triple at most once a scene, and keep 'Suno, suno, suno!' as the one the family quotes back.

'HAAYE' SPELLING. 'Haaye!' is spelled the way Punjabi aunties are spelled in films. On a loud aunt who feeds people, that one word makes her the Bollywood Punjabi aunty, the very type the comics review named. In a Hindi-belt town the same cry is a short 'Haay'. FIX: spell it 'Haay!' in Roman letters (the Devanagari हाय stays), at most once a scene and never just before she holds out food. Keep 'Haay!' in English mode too, the way Mami keeps 'Ish.'. Her English 'Oh!' blurs with Mama ji's 'Oho!', which is her own file's open point.

'AJI' WITH तुम. 'Aji' used with तुम ('Aji, goli khaayi? Nahin? Haaye! Abhi khao!') mixes registers: wives who call a husband 'Aji' say आप to him. FIX: 'Aji, goli khaayi? Nahin? Haay! Abhi khaiye!', with आप in both directions. Or drop 'Aji' and use no address word with तुम.

ENGLISH TAG QUESTIONS. In English mode, 'hai na?' becomes tags like 'Teacher fails today, doesn't she?', which sounds odd. Indian English says 'right?' or 'na?'. FIX: 'Teacher fails today, right? Eat first!', and use 'right?' across her English lines.

notes.name: Mausa ji
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). The most real man in the cast: 'Hain?'; 'Lo. Aadha.'; 'So jao.'; 'Hmm. Ho jayega.'; 'Bench theek hai.'; 'Neend hui?'; 'Ji. Drip theek hai?' said standing; the single missed call that means 'reached'; 'Ok.' an hour late; 'Amma ji ghar. Theek hain.'; 'Wiring abhi nayi lagi thi.'; 'Hain? Sach? Light jalaata hoon.'. His few words stay kind and active, never the silent patriarch.

SORRY. 'Galti hui.' is slightly bookish. Spoken north Indian is 'Galti ho gayi.', which still has no subject. FIX: 'Galti ho gayi.' | 'ग़लती हो गई।' | 'My mistake.' The English 'A mistake.' is clipped to the point of sounding odd.

BRUSHING OFF THANKS. 'Hmm. Kaam tha.' (It was the job) is made up. The real brush-off is 'Isme kya.' FIX: 'Hmm. Isme kya.' | 'हम्म। इसमें क्या।' | 'Hmm. It's nothing.', and then he leaves the room as before.

MOMENT 3. 'Hmm. Naukri. Mazboot.' into the phone is the one place his short style turns into a gimmick: three nouns down a phone line. FIX: 'Achha hai. Lo, Mausi se baat karo.' | 'अच्छा है। लो, मौसी से बात करो।' | 'Good. Here, talk to your Mausi.' Handing the phone over is the deed.

PLATFORM GOODBYE. His goodbye shares Papa's last-coach vigil (cast-wide 6). FIX: he sets the half sweet lime on the seat and walks off before the train moves, the same way he leaves the room when thanked.

notes.name: Masterji
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Bas abhi.' (every player has a tailor who says it, and Sunita will laugh at herself); 'Dekhiye'; 'Waise'; 'Uff.'; 'Bhai sahab, cheeni ungli bhar zyada. Kapda hota, kaat deta.'; 'Apni sadri jaisa. Astar naya, kapda wahi purana.'; 'Geela kapda sookh jaata hai... Fikr phate ki hoti hai.'; giving credit for his wife's buttonholes; typing 'ok ji' with '..' and 'h'. Farida will hear her own bazaar Hindustani, and the file rightly leaves out marked Urdu courtesy words.

WHIMSY ON EVERY LINE. His wander to cloth or weather closes 10 of his 12 test lines. At that rate the charm becomes a stamp, and the sky is sulking every time he speaks. FIX: wander in about one run in two, and let other lines stop at the verdict.

PICTURES NOBODY FOLLOWS. Two pictures make no sense to a Hindi speaker, and players will read them as translated: 'Barsaat mein ghadi bhi phoolti hai.' (clocks swell) and the thanks 'Ab ye tumhari chai wali barsaat.' FIX for the late guest: 'Gaadi late hogi, Captain. Barsaat mein sab late.' | 'गाड़ी लेट होगी, कप्तान। बरसात में सब लेट।' | 'Train must be late, Captain. Everything's late in the rains.' Thanks to you: 'Jeete raho. Us chai ne bachaa liya.' | 'जीते रहो। उस चाय ने बचा लिया।' | 'You're a gem. That tea saved me.' The owner should confirm 'jeete raho' under rule 3. Thanks to Mummy: 'Bhabhi ji, aapki chhat ne bachaa liya. Ehsaan raha.' | 'भाभी जी, आपकी छत ने बचा लिया। एहसान रहा।' | 'Bhabhi ji, your roof saved my cloth. I owe you.'

ENGLISH MODE. 'Mind you,' opens nearly every wander, and 'Uff.' becomes 'Ugh.'. Indian English for 'waise' is 'By the way' or 'Then again', and 'Ugh' is a teenager's disgust, not an old tailor's sigh. FIX: alternate 'By the way,' and 'Then again,', at most once a run, and keep 'Uff.' in English mode, since Indian English speakers say it.

COMMUNITY GUESS. He is the one man allowed soft Urdu-rooted words, and he is a tailor (see cast-wide 8). FIX: keep him unmarked and never comic, and share fikr, waqt and zaroor with others, so his speech marks the town, not a community.

notes.name: Captain sahab
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Straight bat. Front foot.' as his hello; 'Arre waah' said quietly at a clean catch; 'Retired hurt. Sirf ghutna.'; 'Nau matlab nau, Bhai sahab.'; 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.'; 'Ruko. Lineman sahab, aapki batting.'; 'khiladi' for any child; 'Madam ji'; 'Lineman sahab'; texts like 'Happy birthday front foot' and 'Cup 15 aug ground 9 am 🏏'. Ravi and Mr Natarajan will know him.

CRICKET UNCLE CARICATURE. An umpire's call opens 10 of his 12 test lines, and every feeling (sorry, thanks, love, comfort, fear) is an umpire's word. That is the strict-cricket-uncle caricature. A retired bus-depot mechanic talks cricket at the ground and plain Hindi with depot words at the gate. FIX: a call in at most one bubble in two. Moment 2: 'Ab aaye? Catch bhi aise hi chhoota tha.' | 'अब आए? कैच भी ऐसे ही छूटा था।' | 'Now? That's how the catch went too.' Moment 11: 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' | 'कोई बात नहीं, खिलाड़ी। होता है।' | 'Never mind, player. It happens.'

HINDI MODE. Sunita and Meena cannot read टाइम्ड आउट, डेड बॉल, रिटायर्ड हर्ट or वेल फ़ील्डेड. FIX: in Hindi mode, Timed out becomes 'टाइम ख़त्म।'; Dead ball becomes 'ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी।'; Retired hurt becomes 'घुटना छुट्टी पर।'; Well fielded becomes 'अच्छा पकड़ा।'. Keep the English calls in Hinglish and English modes, and keep आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल and फ़्रंट फ़ुट in Hindi.

THE GRUDGE LINE. 'Mera iklauta trial' sounds odd, because 'iklauta' is said of an only child. FIX: 'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' | 'एक ही ट्रायल था। नॉट आउट। किसी से पूछ लो।' | 'One trial. Not out. Ask anyone.'
PROOF CATCHPHRASE. 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' raises the rule 22 problem in cast-wide 5. Keep it for rumours, and never in a chapter that holds a report.
ENGLISH MODE. 'Oh, nice.' for 'Arre waah.' is weak. FIX: 'Shot.', said quietly (the English cricket cry, with no hidden holy word), or keep 'Arre waah.' in English mode the way Mami keeps 'Ish.'.

notes.name: Mami
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Bhaiya ji, beti ka paper kaisa gaya?' (her best line); the icy 'Thank you' to vendors; 'Correct?' (pure Indian office English); 'Aur mehmaan? Approved. Extra thaaliyan tum dhona.'; 'Cheeni, extra. Tumhari guest list jaisi.'; 'Mujhe yakeen hai. Bolo, kya likhoon?'; her ✅ ⏳ ❓ lists; the ✅ under Papa's flower; the 'Beti ka bag' line she never ticks. Shruti has worked with her.

DESK VOICE AT HOME. She uses her desk voice (item, comma, status) for family moments. On a goodbye and a cousin's job it turns her into a spreadsheet: 'Naukri, done. Tick. Somvaar se joining. Sahi?' and 'Ticket, done. Tiffin, done. Your file: open. Always.'. A city manager talks like that at the desk and stops at home. FIX for the job: 'Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.' | 'बधाई हो। जॉइनिंग कब से? सोमवार? बहुत अच्छा।' | 'Congratulations. Joining when? Monday? Very good.' For the goodbye: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Jaldi aana.' | 'टिकट, टिफ़िन, हो गए। जल्दी आना।' | 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Come back soon.' The command marks no gender.

HINDI COMMAS. In Hindi mode the comma pairs ('टेंट, हो गया। रसोइया, पेंडिंग।', 'बत्ती, गई।') are English list punctuation. Spoken Hindi does not pause there, so Sunita will read them as translated. FIX: drop the comma in Hindi mode ('टेंट हो गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी।', 'बत्ती गई।') and keep it in Hinglish and English.

COINED SORRY. 'Mera item tha. Chhoot gaya.' is made up. The natural line already contains her verb. FIX: 'Mujhse chhoot gaya, Didi. Shanivaar likhiye.' | 'मुझसे छूट गया, दीदी। शनिवार लिखिए।' | 'I missed it, Didi. Write Saturday.'

BRUSHING OFF THANKS. 'Thank you counter ke liye hai. Yahan bas tick.' is a speech about her own rule, and nobody talks like that. In Indian families a thank-you between relatives often sounds too formal, and that is the real line. FIX: 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.'

'ISH.' 'Ish.' is a real Bengali sound and the right size for her mother's strand. Hindi-mode players also know the coy 'ishh' of old Hindi films, and laughing at the first slice ('Ish. That wasn't on my list.') will read as that coy sound. FIX: keep 'Ish.' for dismay and sympathy only ('Ish. Bachche ka bukhaar utra?'), and give the first slice no exclamation, just the line.

notes.name: You
problems: RINGS TRUE (keep). 'Sab set.'; 'Badhiya.' said straight or deadpan (both real); 'Pehle ___'; 'Torch main laaun?'; 'Nani, dard? Sach-sach bataiye.'; 'Mummy, cheeni ka stock khatam?'; 'Papa, pahunchkar Reached bhejiye.'; 'Mama ji. Pehle Nani se miliye.'; 'Nani, main bhi.'; and copying each person's typing back to them. Putting the listener's name on every line is how young Indians speak to elders.

STIFF SORRY AND THANKS. The player is 22 to 30 (owner answer 2), yet has the stiffest sorry and thanks in the house: 'Nani, maaf kijiye.' and 'Mausa ji, shukriya.'. A young person at home says 'Sorry, Nani.' and 'Thank you, Mausa ji.'. 'Maaf kijiye' is what you say to a stranger you bumped into, and 'shukriya' to your own uncle sounds formal or filmy to Ravi and Sunita. FIX in Hinglish: 'Nani, sorry. Aap hi sahi thin.' | 'नानी, सॉरी। आप ही सही थीं।' | 'Sorry, Nani. You were right.' (थीं agrees with Nani, not you), and 'Thank you, Mausa ji.' | 'थैंक यू, मौसा जी।' | 'Thanks, Mausa ji.'. Hindi mode may keep माफ़ कीजिए and शुक्रिया. Mausi keeps her tripled 'sorry', so the two still sort apart.

THE REFRAIN. 'Papa, dikhaiye.' is right, but bare; the everyday form adds 'zara'. FIX: 'Papa, zara dikhaiye.' | 'पापा, ज़रा दिखाइए।' | 'Let me see, Papa.' The English 'Let's see' sounds like a quiz host; 'Let me see' is the ordinary phrase.

'LOVELY.' In English mode, 'Lovely.' for 'Badhiya.' sounds British. Indian English says 'Great.', which works both straight and deadpan. FIX: 'Great.' ('Great. Toss indoors, Captain sahab?', 'Great. Write it yourself, scorer.').

MOST STERILE SPEECH. The player may say none of arre, achha, haan ji, chalo, theek hai, pakka or 'thank you'. That makes a 25-year-old's speech the most sterile in the game. FIX: cast-wide 1 and 2 fix it: let the player say 'achha' and 'theek hai', and use English verb + kar, in lines that still mark no gender ('Achha, Mama ji. Call karti...' is out because it marks gender; 'Achha, Mama ji. Sab set.' is in).

voices.name: Nani (नानी), turning 80

voice.register: Low, slow and final, and the shortest speaker in the cast. Her shape is hers alone: one to three fragments to a bubble (not counting an address word), each fragment one to three words and closed with a full stop. The stop is part of the line, the way she ruled off each line of a bill. No commas: every item gets its own stop, because a comma list is Mummy's shape. A verb comes only in an order, a 'who should' ask or a bare fact about herself ('Maine bheja.'). The one whole sentence she allows herself is a real saying from the counter ('Dandi mat maarna.'). Never hurried and never raised, except one 'Bas!' a year. Her questions are 'who should' asks or sly verbless questions handed back to the speaker. Feeling comes out as an order: help becomes a job she hands to 'koi', worry becomes 'Sacks up', care becomes 'I'm right here'. Sly, with a straight face, and never the comic one in her own chapter. Plain once, in the album: 'Aur tum.' She tells time by the lane (after the milk, when the lamps come on, after Mummy's call), never by a clock, and says no figure at all, apart from the album count.
voice.mix: The most Hindi in the cast: the everyday spoken Hindi of a small Hindi-speaking town, full of the counter's idioms. No English verbs, no English clauses, no English tags. English comes only as single nouns the world handed her: doctor, BP, ward, X-ray, ticket, berth, cake, party, flat, list, phone, torch, timetable, and 'scorer' for Tinku. Her Hinglish is her Hindi in Roman letters ('Sab aayein.'), never English with Hindi dropped in. Her images come from the scale and the sacks, never from the account book or a price: तौल, डंडी, तराज़ू, बोरी, छुट्टा, and the goods she weighed out (गुड़, नमक, आटा, घी, राई, जीरा, चीनी). In English mode her lines keep the fragments and the stops, and each saying goes into its plain English sense or the nearest real English idiom ('No thumb on the scale.', 'Weigh your words.'), never a word-for-word oddity.
tics: SHAPE: closed fragments, one to three words each, one to three to a bubble. No comma lists; each item takes its own stop ('Meri gali. Tumhari list.'). A saying keeps its own comma.
VERBS only in orders ('Kaam pe lagao.'), 'who should' asks ('Nani ke saath ghar kaun jaaye?') and bare facts about herself ('Giri nahin. Baith gayi.'). Everything else is nouns: 'Thali thandi.'
ORDERS start with the thing, then the verb or nothing: 'Bori upar.', 'Seedhi. Jaldi.' Never 'look' or 'listen' first (देखो is Masterji's, सुनो is Mausi's).
JOBS go to 'कोई' in the 'should' form, never to a name: 'Koi torch laaye.', 'Koi pakde.'
POSSESSIVES carry her orders: मेरी गली, मेरा बिस्तर, मेरा बटुआ; and 'तुम्हारी लिस्ट' when she hands something over.

THE ONE WHOLE SENTENCE is a real saying from the counter, at most one a scene: 'डंडी मत मारना।', 'राई का पहाड़।', 'बूँद-बूँद से घड़ा भरता है।', 'जितना गुड़, उतना मीठा।', 'आटे में नमक।', 'ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा।', 'दूध का दूध, पानी का पानी।', 'तौल के बोलो।'. A Hindi-first reader confirms each one. She never coins a saying.
SLY TURNS: a verbless question handed back to the speaker ('Suraj bhi aapke timetable se?', 'Chai mein cheeni? Ya cheeni mein chai?').
THIRD PERSON: she calls herself 'Nani' only when she needs help, because she cannot ask for it in the first person ('Who rides home with Nani?').

'BAS.' closes every argument and stands in for 'I'm fine'. The open palm presses down once in the air, then her eyes go to the lane door, where her counter faced (the window is Mausa ji's look when he is moved). One raised 'Bas!' a year.
COUNTS SILENTLY: her left forefinger taps the air once a person, lips moving, no sound. Only the household, never card people. Aloud once in the game, in the album.
TIME BY THE LANE: 'doodh ke baad' (after the milk), 'batti jale' (when the lamps come on), 'phone ke baad' (after Mummy's call). Never a clock time.
ADDRESS BY BIRTH ORDER: बड़ी (Mausi) and छोटे (Mama ji) in Hindi and Hinglish; the tease 'दुकानवाली' for Mummy; 'Scorer' for Tinku in every mode.

TOLD FROM MAUSA JI, the other very short Hindi speaker: she owns things (मेरी, तुम्हारी), says मैं, runs fragments one after another, hands jobs to 'koi' and quotes the counter. He leaves himself out, speaks one verdict on the work ('Mazboot.', 'Dheela.') and lets his hands do the rest.
catchphrases: 'डंडी मत मारना।' | 'Dandi mat maarna.' | 'No thumb on the scale.' The grocer's own idiom (डंडी मारना, to short-weigh), known across the north: do the job honestly and in full. Said before any job she hands over.
'बस।' | 'Bas.' | 'That's that.' ('Enough.' when it stops someone.) Closes every argument and stands in for 'I'm fine', with the palm pressed down once.
'सब आएँ।' | 'Sab aayein.' | 'Everyone comes.' Her want and the game's first message (the phone types it 'सब आएं।'). In the album it turns into 'सब आए।', everyone came.
voice.exclamation: 'Baap re.' | 'बाप रे।' | 'Well I never.' For real astonishment only: news that truly surprises her. Said low and closed with a full stop, never an exclamation mark, so it is the one exclamation in the cast that is not raised. No religious meaning: literally 'O father', an everyday cry of surprise in every community. Never followed by a name, and always in this one form ('Baap re baap' is not used). A power cut or a late guest does not earn it.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: an order, 'Chai piyo.' | 'चाय पियो।' | 'Drink your tea.', with the steel tumbler pushed across. When she is plainly wrong in front of others, she concedes in the scale's words first, then orders the tea: 'Scorer. Tumhara taraazu sachcha. Chai piyo.' Tea now means sorry and nothing else: not comfort, not thanks. THANKS: the next job, 'Ab ye bhi.' | 'अब ये भी।' | 'Now this one too.', the walking stick pointing at it; trusting you with more is her thank-you. Thanked herself, she does the same: 'Rehne do. Ab ye bhi.' | 'Leave it. Now this one too.' LOVE: in words once, the album's 'Aur tum.' | 'और तुम।' | 'And you.' All year it is an order that keeps someone near ('Main yahin. Kahin nahin.') and a touch between painted people: her palm on Mama ji's bent head, a hand on Tinku's shoulder. Never 'sorry', 'thank you' or 'I love you' to family.

गली (the lane)

डंडी (the scale's beam; डंडी मारना, to short-weigh)

सच्चा (true, of a scale or a person)

छुट्टा (change)
गुड़, नमक, आटा, घी, राई, जीरा, चीनी (the goods she weighed, as images)

उधार (credit), only about the credit book she tore up

धीरे (slowly)

English nouns only: doctor, BP, ward, X-ray, ticket, berth, cake, party, flat, list, phone, torch, timetable, scorer
never: प्लीज़ / please, to family
सॉरी / sorry (Mausi's), माफ़ / maaf (yours, 'Maaf kijiye')
थैंक यू, शुक्रिया, धन्यवाद (she thanks with the next job; 'Shukriya' is yours)
मैं ठीक हूँ, सब ठीक, a bare 'ठीक।' (she says बस; 'Theek.' is Mausa ji's)
any figure in speech: a clock time, a price, a score, a head-count, berth arithmetic, an ordinal (पहली included), an age in years. The album count is the one exception
बेटा, बेटी, बच्चा, भैया, दीदी or any gendered or pet word for you; no pet names for anyone
an English verb, clause or tag ('check karo', 'don't worry', 'okay?')
a comma list (Mummy's shape)
शायद / maybe

हिसाब (Mummy's), देखो or देखिए (Masterji's), सुनो (Mausi's), अरे (Captain sahab's 'Arre waah'), चलो (Masterji's sorry), 'पहले ___' (yours), लो and हम्म (Mausa ji's), अभी as a one-word order (Mausa ji's arc word), पक्का, कमाल (Papa's), बहुत याद (Mausi's), हाय, ओहो, 'not out' and 'next ball' (Captain sahab's), 'Correct?' and 'Tick' (Mami's), 'बिल नहीं' (Mummy's), 'haan?' as a tag (Tinku's), 'aur haan' (Mama ji's)
हुक्म or हाज़िर (court and feudal Hindi, the wrong class and region for a small-town grocer)
दाल and मिर्च as images (Papa's dal, Mummy's roof chillies)
haggling, profit or a debt owed to her (the trader stereotype)
a gendered verb about anyone whose gender the story keeps open: 'डॉक्टर की सलाह', 'डॉक्टर ने कहा', never 'डॉक्टर बोले'
any religious word, exclamation or blessing formula (हे भगवान, राम राम, हाय राम, या अल्लाह, God, Lord, Gosh, Heavens, Good grief); बाप रे is never followed by a name
a saying nobody really says: every saying is a real one, read by a Hindi-first reader
बुढ़ापा (old age) about herself, or 'in our day' / हमारे ज़माने में
any word about a woman's dress, anyone's looks, or anyone's caste, religion or region
any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand ('a misunderstanding', 'a family matter', 'keep it quiet'); she is the first to believe
the name or note words of anyone on the coming cards (rule 36)
address: To YOU: तुम, and only in lines that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('काम पे लगाओ।', 'अपनी सुनाओ।'), 'who should' asks ('नानी के साथ घर कौन जाए?') and lines where you are not the doer ('मेरी गली। तुम्हारी लिस्ट।', where तुम्हारी agrees with the list). Never a future or a past about you (करोगे, आ गए). No family word, whatever rulebook Q7 decides, never your name, never बेटा. In the album: 'और तुम।'

Rule 66 checker flags on her lines to or around you, each for a native reader to clear: 'डंडी मत मारना।' (an infinitive command), 'अब ये भी।' (a particle), 'मैं यहीं।' (about her), 'कौन जाए?' and 'कोई लाए।' ('should' forms), 'मैंने भेजा।' (her own act), 'गिरी नहीं। बैठ गई।' (about her), 'पूरा तौल।' (agrees with तौल).
To MUMMY: no word, or the tease 'दुकानवाली' | 'Dukaanwali' | 'Shopkeeper' when she talks prices at home; तुम.
To MAUSI: 'बड़ी' | 'Badi'; तुम. In English mode, no word. 'बड़ी। धीरे।' | 'Slower.' when Mausi starts talking.
To MAMA JI: 'छोटे' | 'Chhote'; तुम. In English mode, no word.
To TINKU: 'स्कोरर' | 'Scorer' in every mode; तुम.

To PAPA, MAUSA JI and MAMI: आप, with no name and the -इए forms ('आप बैठिए।' | 'Aap baithiye.' | 'Do sit.'). Everyone who married in gets आप, as her customers did, women and men alike. Proposed December: her first तुम to all three at once ('तुम सब भी बैठो।' | 'Tum sab bhi baitho.' | 'All of you too. Sit with us.').
To MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: their titles and आप, as elders of the street.
To the LANE: first names, तुम to the younger and आप to her own age.
To the NIGHT NURSE (proposed): आप and the job title the readers settle.
To the DOCTOR: 'डॉक्टर' and आप; she insists the doctor speaks to her ('मुझसे पूछिए।').

habits: DEVICE: the large-screen phone Mama ji gave her (no brand ever named or shown), lying on her lap on speaker. Tinku set up the microphone key and she taught herself the rest, so no one has to read or write for her (her contradiction, on a phone).

SCRIPT: Devanagari only, because she dictates in Hindi, written the way the phone actually produces it: anusvara forms (अस्सीवां, आएं) and English nouns in Devanagari letters (डॉक्टर, बीपी). A Hindi-first reader checks every typed sample against a real phone's voice typing.

SHAPE: the same as her speech. One short phrase at a time, each closed with one firm tap on the full stop (।), the way she ruled off each line of a bill. Voice typing adds no danda by itself, so the stops are hers. No commas, because the stop is the only key she taps. Fragments of one to three words.

NUMBERS: none. The one figure she ever sends is the occasion in the opening message, which the phone writes as it hears it (अस्सीवां or 80वां, checked on a real phone). No time, no price, no BP reading (Mami logs those).
NEVER: a greeting or sign-off, anyone's name, emoji, the folded hands, stickers, forwards or good-morning pictures.

VOICE NOTES: anything longer than three fragments becomes a voice note. It starts with 'हाँ,' as if you had rung her and ends with 'बस।'. Shown as live text on the painted blank phone; the caption is her speech, in standard spelling like her bubbles.
REPLIES: she never answers a text with a text. She phones back, usually within the hour.
WHEN: before seven in the morning and just after the nine o'clock call with Mummy; never after ten, except once, the ward night, which is how Tinku knows she is not sleeping.

THE FAMILY GROUP: Mama ji added her. She reads it on her lap and posts only to stop news she does not want (the fall). The owner ruled out a group chat on screen on 23 Oct, so it exists for the writers only.
HOW YOU TYPE TO HER: you don't. You call, or send a voice note.
samples: To you, January, on screen at 1.01 (voice-typed; the one figure she ever sends). HI: 'अस्सीवां। मई। सब आएं।' | HINGLISH: 'Assiwaan. May. Sab aayein.' | EN: 'My eightieth. May. Everyone comes.'
To you, April (proposed, voice-typed). HI: 'केक नहीं। हलवा। बस।' | HINGLISH: 'Cake nahin. Halwa. Bas.' | EN: 'No cake. Halwa. That's that.' (Mausi has already bought the candles.)

To Tinku, the ward night, past midnight, a voice note shown as live text (her petty fault, seen; she lost that board). HI: 'हाँ, पिछला बोर्ड मेरा। कॉपी ग़लत। बस।' | HINGLISH: 'Haan, pichhla board mera. Copy galat. Bas.' | EN: 'Yes. Last board was mine. Your book's wrong. That's that.'

Family group, off screen, the morning after the fall (voice-typed). HI: 'गिरी नहीं। बैठ गई। कोई न आए। बस।' | HINGLISH: 'Giri nahin. Baith gayi. Koi na aaye. Bas.' | EN: 'Didn't fall. Sat down. Nobody come. That's all.' (Mama ji comes anyway.)
To Mama ji, November (voice-typed). HI: 'फ़ोन बंद। आ जाओ। बस।' | HINGLISH: 'Phone band. Aa jao. Bas.' | EN: 'Stop phoning. Just come. That's all.'
To you, July, the first big rain (voice bank, voice-typed; a 'who should' ask). HI: 'बारिश। छत पर कौन जाए?' | HINGLISH: 'Baarish. Chhat par kaun jaaye?' | EN: 'Rain. Who goes up to the roof?'
To Papa, a voice note answering his good-morning flower (sly). HI: 'हाँ, सुबह हो गई।' | HINGLISH: 'Haan, subah ho gayi.' | EN: 'Yes. It's morning.'

changed: SHAPE MADE HERS ALONE: no commas anywhere; each item takes its own stop, because a comma list is Mummy's target shape ('Meri gali, tumhari list.' becomes 'Meri gali. Tumhari list.'). One to three fragments a bubble, one to three words each. Fixes the C2 look-alike with Mummy.

VERBS ONLY IN ORDERS, 'who should' asks and bare facts about herself: 2.03 'Meri poori gali aayi hai.' becomes 'Meri poori gali.'; 'Doctor ne kaha, ek raat. Maine haan kaha.' becomes 'Raat bhar. Doctor ki salaah. Meri haan.'; 'Beemar hoon, behri nahin.' becomes 'Beemar. Behri nahin.'; the carrom voice note drops 'tha'. Her jokes keep the shape too: 'Aapke timetable se suraj bhi uthta hai?' becomes 'Suraj bhi aapke timetable se?'.

NO NUMBERS IN SPEECH (C1): 'ek raat' becomes 'raat bhar'; both 'Assi' age jokes and the one-candle joke are struck; the one age joke left, for rulebook Q5, has no figure ('Meri umar? Mat taulo. Bhaari.'). The album count is the only figure she ever says, and the opening's अस्सीवां the only one she ever types, marked as the occasion's name for the typing pass.

REAL COUNTER SAYINGS IN PLACE OF HEAD-COUNTS (india review): her one whole sentence is a saying, at most one a scene, from a list of real ones (राई का पहाड़, बूँद-बूँद से घड़ा भरता है, जितना गुड़ उतना मीठा, आटे में नमक, ऊँट के मुँह में जीरा, दूध का दूध पानी का पानी, तौल के बोलो, डंडी मत मारना) for a Hindi-first reader to confirm. None is invented. 'Pehle tolo, phir bolo' is trimmed to 'Taul ke bolo', because 'Pehle ___' is yours.

SORRY, THANKS AND LOVE PULLED APART (C3, C4): tea now means sorry only. The comfort line 'Bas. Main yahin hoon. Chai piyo.' becomes 'Main yahin. Kahin nahin.'; it is not an order to sleep, which is Mausa ji's to you on the same ward night. Thanks is the next job ('Ab ye bhi.'), and it is also how she takes thanks ('Rehne do. Ab ye bhi.'). Love is 'Aur tum.', once. When she is plainly wrong she concedes in the scale's words before the tea ('Tumhara taraazu sachcha.'), so her sorry has a spoken form of its own.

EXCLAMATION 'Baap re.' kept, now given an English mode ('Well I never.') and a rule: said low with a full stop, for real astonishment only, so it is the one unraised exclamation in the cast. A power cut and a late guest no longer earn it.

WORDS GIVEN UP to their new single owners (matrix 2.15): अरे (Captain sahab), चलो (Masterji's sorry), देखो, सुनो, हिसाब, the 'बस, सब ठीक' she said to Mama ji ('Theek.' is Mausa ji's, so it becomes plain 'Bas.'), 'Pehle', 'Abhi' as a one-word order (Mausa ji's arc word, so 'Ladder. Now.' becomes 'Seedhi. Jaldi.' | 'Ladder. Quick.', and his file, which quotes it, updates), and every ordinal including पहली. Dal and mirch are kept out of her images (Papa's dal, Mummy's chillies).

BODY TELL MOVED OFF MAUSA JI'S: after 'Bas.' her eyes now go to the lane door her counter faced, not the window, which is where Mausa ji looks when he is moved. A told-apart note against Mausa ji, the other very short Hindi speaker, is added to her habits.

TRADER STEREOTYPE (C11): her images are the scale and the sacks (weighing true, honest measure), never haggling, profit or a debt owed to her; उधार stays only for the credit book she tore up, and no price is ever said.

'KOI' JOBS MADE CLEAR in Hindi: a bare 'Koi torch.' reads as 'some torch', so jobs take the 'should' form ('Koi torch laaye.', 'Koi kapda laaye.', 'Koi pakde.'), which rule 66 already clears as in its own example कौन लाए?.

HEARD WITH OTHERS (C15): eight of the twelve test lines go to someone other than you (the table, Mama ji twice, the cousin, Mausi, Tinku, the neighbour, the child), so the blind sort hears her address words (बड़ी, छोटे, Scorer) as well as her shape.

TYPING: no commas in typed messages either (she taps only the stop); the carrom voice note is in fragments; a July rain message with a 'who should' ask is added for the voice bank; the opening's figure is marked as the one she ever sends.

KEPT, and why: essence, want, fear and contradiction (help turned into her own order, the third-person 'Nani' when she needs help); 'Sab aayein', 'Dandi mat maarna', 'Bas'; the silent finger count and the album's spoken count; बड़ी, छोटे, दुकानवाली and 'Scorer'; आप to all three in-laws and the December first तुम; every rule 22 and rule 3 guard. One flag for readers: in the album's Hinglish 'Ek, do, teen', 'do' (two) can be read as the English verb, though the counting run makes it clear.

voices.name: Mummy (मम्मी), 52

voice.register: Brisk, mid-fast and level: the pace of a shop counter on a Saturday, warm underneath, never cold, never loud. MEDIUM length, the middle of the cast: one bubble of five to ten words, made of one list of people and jobs (or goods) joined by commas and closed by one full stop ('Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.'). A second thought is a second bubble, never a longer one. Her list is not Nani's closed one-to-three-word fragments, not Captain sahab's call and then a reason, not Mami's 'thing, status' items or readback, and not Papa's run of whole sentences. A list may carry one verb, and then it is often the English verb + kar/ho ('check karo'). HUMOUR: none on purpose. She is the straight face; the family laughs at her shop voice at home ('Haan ji, boliye' to her own children, 'Aur kuch?' at a goodbye) and she never hears the joke. FEELING is changed into shop news with no figure ('Copper phir mehenga.'); love stays a deed. CROSS: very still, the voice drops, and politeness rises. The one slow subject is her roof chillies: there the list stops and she says one whole, unhurried sentence.
voice.mix: A Hindi frame (the everyday Hindi of a small Hindi-speaking town) with English nouns from today's counter dropped in whole: shutter, stock, bill, counter, delivery, godown, customer, fuse, wire, switch, fan, bulb, copper, MCB, mains, extension, credit book. Hers alone in the cast is the English verb + kar/ho: 'check karo', 'count karo', 'lock karo', 'return karo', 'mains off karo', 'scan karke', 'delivery ho gayi'. No whole English clauses: Mama ji and Mami switch clause by clause. What her English carries: goods. Hindi mode keeps the trade nouns in Devanagari as Hindi speakers say them (शटर, स्टॉक, बिल, चेक करो). English mode keeps the comma list and the rising 'ji' on names (Tinku ji, Chhote ji), and renders 'Haan ji, boliye' as 'Yes, go ahead' and 'Aur kuch?' as 'Anything else?'. Her two marked figures are said in words in speech ('nau baje', 'nau bajkar das'), which collide with no other word (unlike 'saath'); in typing a figure is a digit.
tics: Answers every phone call with the shop greeting, 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, go ahead.', to Nani and to you exactly as to a customer, and carries on without correcting herself. This is her first tell.

Speaks in one comma list of people and jobs, five to ten words, ticking the items off on the fingers of her left hand: 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.' Comfort, a no and a goodbye all come out in this one shape.

Closes a talk the way she closes a sale: 'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?', after a compliment, at a goodbye, when asked how she is. At most one bubble in four, because Mami's 'Correct?' holds the cast's other closing question.
Changes a feeling into shop news with no figure: 'How are you, Mummy?' 'Copper phir mehenga.' The dodge is hers alone; Papa and Tinku drop theirs (C10).
The English verb + kar/ho, hers alone, used on home things as on stock: a too-sweet cup of tea gets 'ye cup return karo', a power cut at dinner gets 'MCB check karo'.
When cross, politeness rises instead of volume: 'ji' goes onto names that never carry it ('Tinku ji', 'Chhote ji'), तुम becomes आप, commands become -इए and -लीजिए, and her hands clasp at her waist.
Gives the hour in whole hours by her father's watch, which runs two minutes fast ('nau baje'). Minutes only in an emergency ('Nau bajkar das.'), which is how the family knows it is one.
On the roof, with the chillies, the list stops: one slow whole sentence with a verb ('Mirchi bach gayi.'). It is the only time she speaks slowly.
Counts heads with one raised left forefinger, exactly as Nani does, in silence: the count is never said aloud (a head-count in speech is Nani's one album line).
catchphrases: 'Haan ji, boliye.' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए।' | 'Yes, go ahead.' (every phone call, every customer, and you)
'Nau baje. Shutter up.' | 'नौ बजे। शटर ऊपर।' | 'Nine o'clock. Shutter up.' (her one catchphrase with a number: the shutter hour, which her target allows)
'Iska bill nahin.' | 'इसका बिल नहीं।' | 'There's no bill for this.' (her thank-you, hers alone)
voice.exclamation: 'Had hai!' | 'हद है!' | 'That's the limit!' For exasperation only: the water at the door, the lights failing in an electrician's own house, a delivery gone wrong. Secular: it means 'this is the limit', no god is in it, and it is never followed by any name. No one else in the cast uses it. She has no exclamation for joy: good news comes out as orders ('Tinku, mithai lao.').
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, said out loud as a debt she takes on: 'Ye mere hisaab mein.' | 'ये मेरे हिसाब में।' | 'Put that on my account.' It is the only line where she says हिसाब. THANKS, a thing off the shelf with no bill: 'Iska bill nahin.' | 'इसका बिल नहीं।' | 'There's no bill for this.' (hers alone; Masterji drops 'Paise nahin loonga'). When someone thanks her she says the same words and turns straight to the next job ('Tinku, agle ka bill banao.'). LOVE, never in words: the red 'paid' pen laid down for you in January and the spare shop key laid down in the album, each turned towards you, her hand coming back to her side. When love has to come out in speech, it is a packed list of goods ('Torch, charger, extension, sab bag mein. Aur kuch?') or a list of jobs that hands you the shop ('Baaki mahine, baaki phone, sab tumhare.').

'ye wala' | 'ये वाला' | 'this one' (the thing in her hand or in the photo)
'Aur kuch?' | 'और कुछ?' | 'Anything else?' (the counter's closer)

'Ek rupaya kam nahin.' | 'एक रुपया कम नहीं।' | 'Not one rupee short.' (her highest praise; 'ek' is idiom, not a count)
Shanivaar, nau baje | शनिवार, नौ बजे | Saturday, nine o'clock (the shutter hour)

'Udhaar? Kal.' | 'उधार? कल।' | 'Credit? Tomorrow.' (the old shop saying, to a stranger only, rare, said flat and never for a laugh, never in the flood week, when the credit book opens to the whole lane)

minutes outside an emergency (Papa's), a score or 'not out' (Tinku's and Captain sahab's), an ordinal (nobody's), a head-count said aloud (Nani's, once)
'sorry' (Mausi's), 'maaf kijiye' and 'shukriya' (yours), 'thank you', 'dhanyavaad'
'chinta mat karo' | 'don't worry' (Mama ji's line; she distrusts it); 'help' or 'madad' about herself; 'thak gayi' | 'I'm tired'; a vague time ('lagbhag', 'thodi der mein', 'around ten')

words other people own: 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' as one-word lines, 'Galti hui', 'Mazboot' (Mausa ji); 'galat', 'Kamaal', 'Noted', 'Reached?' (Papa); 'Pehle ___' (yours); 'pakka', 'aur haan', 'Oho' (Mama ji); 'suno' as an opener, 'hai na?', 'bahut yaad', 'Haaye' (Mausi); 'haan?' as a tag, 'Gazab' (Tinku); 'Correct?', 'Tick', 'pending', 'done' as statuses, 'Ish', 'Bhaiya ji' (Mami); 'Dekhiye', 'Chalo', 'Uff' (Masterji); 'arre' as an exclamation, 'Next ball' (Captain sahab); 'Bas.', 'Chai piyo', 'Baap re' (Nani)
her old 'Theek hai, toh...' lead-in (too close to Mausa ji's 'Theek.')
'saath' in Hinglish (it reads as both 60 and 'with', the india review)
a joke on purpose, a tease for laughs, 'special price for you', haggling, or any line that makes her the greedy trader (realism notes, caricature traps)
a whole English clause ('Don't worry, I'll handle it' belongs to Mama ji)
any god-word or religious exclamation, any caste word, any brand (rule 3); English-mode mild oaths too (Gosh, Heavens, Good grief, Thank God)
any pet name or gendered word for you: beta | बेटा, bachcha | बच्चा, raja, gudiya, भैया, दीदी (rules 8, 66)
a word on anyone's character beyond counter habits, or anything about women or men in general (rule 22)
any doubt of a report of harassment or bullying, or of a dowry demand, or 'misunderstanding' | 'ग़लतफ़हमी' about one (rule 22)
a thumbs-up or any emoji (Mausa ji's and yours)
address: To you: तुम in commands (देखो, गिनो, भेजो, लॉक करो), in 'who should' asks (किसे रखें?, कौन करे?, never कौन करेगा?) and in lines where you are not the doer (बाक़ी फ़ोन, सब तुम्हारे।); आप and -इए only when she is cross (आप ही गिन लीजिए।). No address word for you at all: never beta or a pet name, never बेटा, भैया or दीदी. Her shop greeting reaches you on the phone too, and बोलिए marks no gender.
To Nani: 'Amma' | 'अम्मा', with आप ('Amma, aap baithiye.'), the word all three of Nani's children use.
To Papa: no address word; she starts with the item ('Bhindi itni mehngi?'), with तुम, equal respect. Of him, to you and Tinku: 'tumhare Papa'.
To Mama ji: 'Chhote' | 'छोटे', with तुम; 'Chhote ji' and आप when cross (and when he arrives late).
To Mausi: 'Didi' | 'दीदी', with आप.
To Mausa ji: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी', with आप.
To Tinku: 'Tinku', with तुम; 'Tinku ji' and आप when cross, in speech and in typing.
To Mami: 'Bhabhi' | 'भाभी', with तुम; 'tumhari Mami' when she speaks of her to you.
To Masterji and Captain sahab: their titles, with आप; both call her 'Bhabhi ji'.
To customers, wholesalers and hired hands: 'ji' and आप, always ('Haan ji, boliye.', 'Le jaiye, ji.'), with no kin word, so 'Bhaiya ji' stays Mami's.
samples: ORDER (to you and Tinku, Saturday, before the shutter): 'Tum bill, Tinku stock, main shutter.' | 'तुम बिल, टिंकू स्टॉक, मैं शटर।' | 'You on bills, Tinku on stock, me on the shutter.' (her signature shape: people and jobs in one comma list, verbless; no rule 66 flag)

THE GOAL OF THE MOMENT (chapter 3 opening, rules 37 and 43): 'Kichad saaf, maal upar, Shanivaar nau baje shutter.' | 'कीचड़ साफ़, माल ऊपर, शनिवार नौ बजे शटर।' | 'Mud out, stock up, shutter at nine on Saturday.' (the shutter hour, one of her two marked figures, as the chapter's target; never the number the two tie on)

A 'WHO SHOULD' ASK (chapter 3, to you): 'Haath chahiye, kichad aur maal ke liye. Kise rakhein?' | 'हाथ चाहिए, कीचड़ और माल के लिए। किसे रखें?' | 'Hands needed, mud and stock. Who do we take on?' (रखें is a subjunctive and marks no gender; no flag)

TO A CUSTOMER (the counter, any day): 'Haan ji, boliye. Fuse, switch ya wire?' | 'हाँ जी, बोलिए। फ़्यूज़, स्विच या वायर?' | 'Yes, go ahead. Fuse, switch or wire?' (the shop greeting, then the list as a question)

TO THE WHOLESALER'S MAN who asks for the 'malik': 'Main hi hoon. Boliye, delivery kab?' | 'मैं ही हूँ। बोलिए, डिलीवरी कब?' | 'You're looking at her. Go ahead: when's the delivery?' (one beat at most, no general statement; straight to business)

WORRY (the flood, to Masterji over the wall): 'Masterji, fan, wire, switch, sab paani mein. Poora maal.' | 'मास्टरजी, फ़ैन, वायर, स्विच, सब पानी में। पूरा माल।' | 'Masterji, fans, wire, switches, all under water. The whole stock.' (replaces 'Pachaas hazaar.': the worry is the goods, not a sum)

WORRY, AN EMERGENCY (any night, to you): 'Nau bajkar das. Amma ka phone nahin aaya.' | 'नौ बजकर दस। अम्मा का फ़ोन नहीं आया।' | 'Ten past nine. Amma hasn't rung.' (emergency minutes, her second marked figure: Nani rings at nine, so silence is the alarm; check 3 flags आया, which agrees with फ़ोन, so a native reader clears it)

THE DODGE (asked how she is): 'Copper phir mehenga. Aur kuch?' | 'कॉपर फिर महँगा। और कुछ?' | 'Copper's up again. Anything else?' (a feeling changed into shop news with no figure, closed like a sale; check 3 flags महँगा, which agrees with कॉपर, so a native reader clears it)

PRAISE (to you, after you count the drawer at closing): 'Ek rupaya kam nahin. Galla lock karo, shutter neeche.' | 'एक रुपया कम नहीं। गल्ला लॉक करो, शटर नीचे।' | 'Not one rupee short. Lock the drawer, shutter down.' (her highest praise, then the next job; 'ek' is idiom, not a count; check 3 flags नीचे, an adverb that agrees with nothing, so a native reader clears it)

THANKS (to Mausi after the flood basket, handing her a new emergency light off the shelf): 'Didi, ye rakhiye. Iska bill nahin.' | 'दीदी, ये रखिए। इसका बिल नहीं।' | 'Didi, keep this. There's no bill for it.' (her thank-you, hers alone)

SORRY (to Masterji, the morning after she sent him back on the first flood night): 'Masterji, kal raat ki zid, ye mere hisaab mein.' | 'मास्टरजी, कल रात की ज़िद, ये मेरे हिसाब में।' | 'Masterji, last night's stubbornness: put that on my account.' (her sorry, said out loud as a debt she takes on; the only line where she uses हिसाब)

SAYING NO (to Mama ji, who has sent money again): 'Chhote, paise apne paas rakho, khud aao, Amma ke paas.' | 'छोटे, पैसे अपने पास रखो, ख़ुद आओ, अम्मा के पास।' | 'Chhote, keep your money, come yourself, see Amma.' (a no as a list of jobs)

GIVING CREDIT (the flood week, to a stranger from the lane who needs a fuse): 'Le jaiye, ji. Credit book mein likh diya, aaram se.' | 'ले जाइए, जी। क्रेडिट बुक में लिख दिया, आराम से।' | 'Take it, ji. It's in the credit book. No hurry.' (her turn in chapter 3: owing the lane is how a lane works; the shop is never the stingy-trader joke)

CROSS (to Tinku, five past nine on a Saturday): 'Tinku ji, nau baj gaye. Aap kahaan hain?' | 'टिंकू जी, नौ बज गए। आप कहाँ हैं?' | 'Tinku ji, it's nine. Where are you, may I ask?' (politeness rises: 'ji' on a name that never carries it, आप; the shutter hour)

CROSS (to Mama ji, who offers to send city workmen): 'Chhote ji, aap hi chala lijiye. Chaabi ye rahi.' | 'छोटे जी, आप ही चला लीजिए। चाबी ये रही।' | 'Chhote ji, you run it, then. Here's the key.' (anger as politeness; the keys held out, then her fist closes on them)

EXCLAIMING (the water at the door, the first flood night): 'Had hai! Paani darwaze tak. Balti, kapda, mains off karo.' | 'हद है! पानी दरवाज़े तक। बाल्टी, कपड़ा, मेन्स ऑफ़ करो।' | 'That's the limit! Water's at the door. Buckets, mains off.' (her one exclamation, then the list; a command, no flag)

COMFORT (to you, the first flood night, at two): 'Paani kal, maal parson, shutter Shanivaar.' | 'पानी कल, माल परसों, शटर शनिवार।' | 'Water out tomorrow, stock the day after, shutter Saturday.' (comfort as a schedule, one comma list; verbless, no flag)

TO PAPA (home with vegetables; no address word, she starts with the item): 'Bhindi itni mehngi? Kal se sabzi main laaungi.' | 'भिंडी इतनी महँगी? कल से सब्ज़ी मैं लाऊँगी।' | 'Okra, that dear? I'm buying the vegetables from tomorrow.' (replaces 'Bhindi 60 rupaye?': she still prices aloud, with no figure; meant, not a tease)

THE ROOF (3.11, the first sun after the flood, an aside and never an ask; her one slow line): 'Mirchi bach gayi. Dabbon mein paani bhara tha, phir bhi.' | 'मिर्ची बच गई। डब्बों में पानी भरा था, फिर भी।' | 'The chillies made it, with the tins full of water.' (the list stops and she speaks whole sentences, slowly; if said in your hearing, check 3 flags गई and भी and check 2 flags भरा था; they belong to मिर्ची, a particle and पानी, so a native reader clears them)

LAYING THE PEN DOWN (1.05, January, a proposed rewrite in her shape): 'Baaki mahine, baaki phone, sab tumhare.' | 'बाक़ी महीने, बाक़ी फ़ोन, सब तुम्हारे।' | 'The other months, the other calls, all yours.' (she assigns, she never asks; replaces 'And the rest? Everyone calls you anyway.'; check 3 flags तुम्हारे, which agrees with महीने and फ़ोन, so a native reader clears it)

SAID DEAD STRAIGHT (1.02, hanging the calendar; waits on rulebook Q5): 'Calendar muft. Keel ka bill alag.' | 'कैलेंडर मुफ़्त। कील का बिल अलग।' | 'The calendar's free. The nail's billed separately.' (she means it and the family laughs: the joke is theirs, not hers; replaces 'Keel ke paanch rupaye.')

THE ALBUM (owner option only; by default she lays the spare key down, turned towards you, and says nothing): 'Shanivaar ka shutter, chaabi, galla, sab tumhare.' | 'शनिवार का शटर, चाबी, गल्ला, सब तुम्हारे।' | 'Saturday's shutter, the key, the drawer, all yours.' (closes January's 'sab tumhare' on the same three words; check 3 flags तुम्हारे, which agrees with the list, so a native reader clears it)

habits: Device: a plain black Android phone in a plain black case, the screen painted blank with every word laid on as live text (rule 30). It lives in the side pocket of her kameez and comes out wedged between her left ear and shoulder.

Script: Roman Hinglish (Hindi in Latin letters), all lowercase. Commas only: no full stops, no question marks, no exclamation marks, even when she asks ('khud kab aa rahe'). Her spelling drifts (chabi, chaabi); her trade nouns never do.

HER TELL, which nobody else in the cast has: she acknowledges everything with the shop greeting typed, 'haan ji', to her own children as to a customer. Never 'ok', never 'done', never a thumbs-up. This replaces the old tell of ending every message on a figure, which broke the cast's number cap on screen.

Shape: the same comma list of people and jobs as her speech ('daal tum banao, shutter neeche, ghar aa rahi'), two to eight words, one message per thought, never a paragraph, never a greeting or a sign-off.

Figures: only when the fact itself is a figure and only in an emergency, so a digit from her is rare and means trouble (the flood night's '6 baje'). Prices stay on the photographed bills, painted blank.
When cross, her texts get polite too: 'ji' on the name and -इए on the verb ('tinku ji counter pe aaiye').
Photos: of bills and stock cartons, painted blank, each with the same caption, 'ye wala check karo' or 'ye wala'.
Voice notes when her hands are busy in the shop. They start with her shop greeting even though she is the one calling ('haan ji boliye, achha tum'), shown as live text.

Emoji: none, ever (the thumbs-up is Mausa ji's, and your own reply to her). No stickers, no good-morning pictures (those are Papa's). The one news she sends unasked is the power-cut times, retyped the moment she hears them, shown as a message card (no group chat appears in the game).

Speed: reads within a minute between nine in the morning and half past eight at night, and replies only when she has the answer. Nothing between the shutter coming down and the end of Nani's nine o'clock call, and never after nine, so a late message from her means trouble. The flood night is the one time all year.
She never texts Nani. Nani rings her at nine every night, and Mummy waits for it.
Types fast with her left thumb, phone in her left hand, because her right hand is holding the keys or the pen.

FEELING (C3, C10). The dodge keeps its shop words and loses its figure: 'Copper phir mehenga.'. A NEW COUNTER CLOSER, 'Aur kuch?' ('Anything else?'). It gives her a tell that is neither a number nor a trade noun, and it carries the target's 'humour none on purpose': her shop voice at home is the family's joke, never hers. 'arre' left her voice note ('arre tum' becomes 'achha tum'; Captain sahab owns 'arre'); 'Theek hai, toh...' is dropped (Mausa ji owns 'Theek.'); 'pakka', 'suno', 'Pehle', 'galti', 'galat' and 'saath' are on her never list; 'Ek, do, teen' head-counting leaves her uses (head-counts in speech are Nani's one album line), and her one-finger count stays a silent gesture.

Everyone calls you anyway.' is proposed as 'Baaki mahine, baaki phone, sab tumhare.', in her list shape, and the album's owner option becomes 'Shanivaar ka shutter, chaabi, galla, sab tumhare.', closing January on the same three words with no figure.
