Amma ka phone nahin aaya.', 'Chhote ji, aap hi chala lijiye.', 'Mirchi bach gayi.' (3.11), and the address table.

UNCHANGED, ON PURPOSE. Her essence (she runs the family like the shop), want (the shutter at nine, owing no one), fear (the shutter staying down, owing anyone), contradiction (swore never to sit behind a counter like her mother, runs hers exactly like her), the cost of her pride on the first flood night, her exclamation 'Had hai!', her rising politeness when cross, and her English verb + kar/ho mix.

FOR THE READERS (rule 65). A Hindi-first reader checks 'Ye mere hisaab mein.' reads as taking the fault and not as trade talk, that 'Aur kuch?' at a goodbye lands as her and not as coldness, and clears every rule 66 flag noted on the samples and test lines (महँगा, नीचे, तुम्हारे, आया, गई, भरा था, गया, जी, भी, मेरी: each agrees with a thing or is a particle or adverb, never with you).

voices.name: Papa (पापा), 56

voice.register: Measured, even and quiet; never raised and never an exclamation mark (chapter 1's one shout is Mausi's). He talks like a platform announcement: an ordered run of whole sentences, each three to eight words with its verb and its full stop, one fact to a sentence, given one after another across one to three bubbles, and the last one names what comes next ('Ab checker aayega.'). That is his long shape, and it is unlike the other three long talkers: Mama ji trails on with commas and 'aur haan', Mausi triples and overlaps, Masterji gives a verdict and wanders into cloth and weather; Papa closes each sentence before he starts the next. Slow and exact. His only verbless lines are the time correction ('9:40, aaspaas nahin.') and the time stamp that opens his thanks. With Nani, who lets him finish, the run is longest (three bubbles); with everyone else it is usually two sentences. Numbers: one of the two people in the cast who lean on them (with Tinku), and only minutes, clock times and the count before a noun; never prices, scores or ordinals. Budget: at most one figure a bubble, and at least one bubble in three with none (in the test set below, 5 lines of 12 carry a figure). Humour is deadpan, about himself and clocks, delivered in the same flat announcement voice.
voice.mix: Careful standard Hindi of the railway colonies, belonging to no one town: full verbs, -इए to elders, no regional colour. English only for railway nouns every Indian traveller knows (coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket, running status, checker) and for clock times, which stay figures in all three modes ('9:40'). His verbs stay Hindi, many of them the railway's own (gaadi lagna, chhootna, chalna, chart banna, berth milna); he never builds a verb from an English word plus kar or ho, which is now Mummy's frame alone. So his praise is 'Sab confirm hai.' (the railway status word) instead of 'Confirm ho gaya.', and his thanks is 'Darj hai.' (entered, the parcel register's word) instead of 'Noted.' or 'note kar liya'. He switches by single nouns, as older speakers do in the Dehradun study the realism notes cite, never by whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami do that). Tamil only in the coach count under his breath, kept in Tamil in every mode (a Tamil reader signs off the words and the script). When cross the English goes altogether: 'late' becomes 'der', 'halt' goes, and only the minutes stay. His typed messages are English (see typing); in English mode his spoken 'Darj hai.' is 'Noted.'
tics: Announces in order: whole sentences, one fact each, each closed with a full stop, the last naming the next step with 'ab ... aayega' | 'अब ... आएगा' | '... comes next' ('Ab checker aayega.' | 'The ticket checker comes next.'). He names the next item before anyone answers.
Corrects any vague time to the minute: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, not "around".' He hears 'about', 'around' and 'lagbhag' as errors; quoting the word back is the only time he says it.
The count before the thing: 'Hum solah log hain.' | 'Four trains this year.' (his alone: Tinku and Mama ji drop number-first).
Names a train by its time: '9:40 wali', '8:15 wali' ('the 9:40'), as railway people do.
Gives the minutes where others give feelings: two hours late is '120 minute'; good news is the minute it came ('Khabar 11:52 par aayi.').

Deadpan jokes in the station loudspeaker's frame: 'Kripya dhyan dein.' | 'Attention, please.' then a home fact ('Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.'). At most once a chapter, never while he asks (rule 37), all of it waiting on rulebook Q5.
Never describes a person's temperament; he logs what they did, with the minute.
Counts the coaches under his breath in Tamil as a train comes in: '...naalu, anju, aaru.' (a whisper bubble; proposal, a Tamil reader signs off).
Looks up for a clock before he speaks in any new place (a gesture in the panel, not a word).
When cross: the minutes left, then one word said twice ('Koi neeche na utre. Koi nahin.'), the guard's flat hand lowered palm down; quieter, never louder, and the English goes.

His judging notes on cards: one time stamp, then the act, in the Hindi transitive past so a note reads the same of a woman or a man; no ordinal and no second figure: '10:20. Asked the coach number again.' | '10:20। फिर से डिब्बे का नंबर पूछा।'; '11:55. Changed seats again.' | '11:55। फिर सीट बदली।'; '1:40. Woke everyone for tea.' | '1:40। चाय के लिए सबको जगाया।'; '12:10. Repacked the bag again.' | '12:10। फिर से बैग बाँधा।'; '9:50. Finished all the snacks.' | '9:50। सारा नाश्ता ख़त्म किया।'; '10:00 onwards. Hummed the same tune.' | '10:00 से। वही धुन गुनगुनाई।'. Never on a decision whose task the note bears on (rule 20), as often on women as on men, lengths kept even within a decision (story_take.length_faults).
catchphrases: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, आसपास नहीं।' | '9:40, not "around".' (the correction; his one catchphrase with a number in it, said whenever anyone gives a time with 'around' or 'about' in it; it replaces '9:40, not 9:45.', which held two figures; the owner may keep the old line as a marked exception)
'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.' | 'नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है।' | 'No. The chart is made.' (his final no: once the railway chart is made, nothing changes)

'Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. / Swaad se banti hai.' | 'दाल घड़ी देखकर नहीं बनती। / स्वाद से बनती है।' | 'Dal is not made by the clock. / It is made by taste.' (when anyone asks how long the dal takes: the one thing he will not time)
voice.exclamation: 'Kamaal hai.' | 'कमाल है।' | English mode 'Remarkable.' New. Said flat, with a full stop and never an exclamation mark, a whole sentence that keeps its verb. Two uses: real surprise at good news ('Kamaal hai. Khabar 11:52 par aayi.') and dry irony ('Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat bana? Kamaal hai.', the power cut that came on time). No religious meaning: 'kamaal' is an everyday word for a wonder or a feat. His alone: Mama ji's 'Kamaal!' goes (matrix 2.15). The English rendering avoids every mild word that hides a holy name (Gosh, Goodness, Good grief).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: he corrects the record against himself, as a fact, the time first, then the right fact: '9:40 mera time tha. / Galat nikla. / Board par 9:25 hai.' | '9:40 मेरा टाइम था। / ग़लत निकला। / बोर्ड पर 9:25 है।' | '9:40 was my time. / It was wrong. / The board says 9:25.' Never 'sorry' (Mausi's alone), never 'Galti hui' (Mausa ji's), never 'Maaf kijiye' (yours). THANKS: he logs the deed with its minute, then 'Darj hai.' (it is entered): 'Mummy ji, 5:52 par chai seedhi par thi. / Darj hai.' | 'मम्मी जी, 5:52 पर चाय सीढ़ी पर थी। / दर्ज है।' | 'Mummy ji, the tea was on the step at 5:52. / Noted.' When he is thanked, the same word and then the next job: 'Darj hai. Ab wapsi ka ticket aayega.' | 'Noted. The return tickets come next.' The family knows 'Darj hai.' is his thank-you. LOVE: never said in words. A deed done ahead of time, announced as a plain fact ('Didi, neeche ki berth aapki hai. / March mein hi ho gayi thi.'); 'Reached?' typed after any journey you make without him (his alone); standing on the platform till the last coach has gone ('Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.'), the colony-gate boy grown up. The nearest he comes to pride is the album's count: 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.'
uses: Clock times in figures, to the minute: 9:40, 6:35, 5:52, 8:55; minutes for any delay ('120 minute')
ab ... aayega | अब ... आएगा | ... comes next
Sab confirm hai | सब कन्फ़र्म है | It is all confirmed (his highest praise)
Darj hai | दर्ज है | Noted (his thanks, and his answer to being thanked)
Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai | नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है | No. The chart is made
Kamaal hai | कमाल है | Remarkable
Kripya dhyan dein | कृपया ध्यान दें | Attention, please (only to open a joke)
Railway Hindi verbs: gaadi lag gayi (drawn up at the platform), gaadi chhooti, gaadi chali, chart ban gaya, berth mil gayi
'9:40 wali' (a train named by its time)

Railway nouns: gaadi, maal gaadi (goods train), dibba and aakhri dibba (coach, the last coach), patri (track), coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket, checker, running status, board
His past: pitaji (his father, a goods-train guard), colony ka gate, guard
The dal: dal, swaad (taste), ghadi dekhkar (by the clock, which is how it is not made)
Mummy ji, Didi, Bhai sahab, Captain sahab, Masterji (with आप); Tinku (तुम)
never: about, roughly, around, nearly | लगभग, क़रीब, आसपास | lagbhag, kareeb (except quoting the word back in his correction); a script can check his lines for these
sharp, theek, theek-theek as a time word ('theek 6:00'): 'sharp' was worn out by three askers and 'Theek.' is Mausa ji's
'pehle' in the 'X first' sense, or 'pehle se': 'Pehle ___' is yours alone
An English verb with kar or ho: 'confirm ho gaya', 'book kiya', 'note kar liya', 'check karo' (Mummy's frame)
'jaldi karo' or any 'hurry up': he says the minutes left instead
'I missed you', 'I'm proud of you', 'love', or any word about his own feelings
English 'sorry' (Mausi's), 'Galti hui' (Mausa ji's), 'thank you' (Mami's, to strangers), 'Shukriya' and 'Maaf kijiye' (yours)
'Don't worry' (Mama ji's), 'ho jayega' with no time in it, 'pakka'
Other people's words: 'Lo.', 'arre', 'haan?', 'hai na?', 'aur haan', 'Dekhiye', 'Suno', 'not out', 'full', 'Next ball'
Prices or money (Mummy's), scores or cricket words (Tinku's and Captain sahab's), ordinals or numbered items (nobody's in speech)
Two figures in one bubble (the only exception is the Tamil whisper count)
beta, or any word for you that fixes gender (rule 8; rulebook Q7)
A Hindi form that marks your gender: no -ोगे/-ोगी future, no 'pahunch gaye/gayi', no 'thak gaye', no 'kaun jaayega?' (rule 66); questions to you use the subjunctive ('कौन रखे?')
Whether you travel on his pass: the pass rules treat a grown son and a grown daughter differently (rule 8)
A temperament word about anyone: moody, shy, emotional, bossy, lazy
Anything that doubts a report of harassment, of being followed, or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22)
A rule for choosing in his ask; only the goal of the moment, never the number the two tie on (rule 37); a card person's name or a card note's words in any bubble (rule 36)
A joke while he asks (rule 37); a joke at anyone's cost
Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar; in English mode no Gosh, Goodness, Good grief, Thank God
Slang: chill, bro, scene, whatever
A shout bubble, an exclamation mark, or a year on screen (rules 2 and 35)
address: YOU: तुम only in lines that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('सो लो', 'देखो'), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive ('चेकर के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।', 'तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।'). Possessives agree with the thing, not you ('बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है', flagged by check 2 and cleared). No name, no beta, no family word; he often opens with the time instead of 'you'. You answer 'Ji Papa' and आप, exactly as you speak to Mummy.
NANI: 'Mummy ji', आप and -इए ('Mummy ji, aap baithiye.'). She is the one he talks to most and longest, because she lets him finish. Readers confirm the word carries no community lean.
MUMMY: no address word; he opens with the time ('Nau baj gaye.'); both say तुम, so the game's own couple carries no honorific-to-husband pattern.
MAMA JI: to his face तुम and no name (the household has no first names); to you he is 'Mama ji'. Mama ji calls him 'Jija ji'.
TINKU: 'Tinku', तुम.
MAUSI: 'Didi', आप. MAUSA JI: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Both wait on the Hindi-first and South Indian readers (rule 65) and the one family address table.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: by their titles, आप.
MAMI: no name, आप (his formality, even to a younger in-law).
A CHILD: commands only ('Gilaas seedha karo.'), so no gender.
STRANGERS AND CARD PEOPLE: आप and 'ji', always; to the ticket checker the count comes first: 'Ji, S4 mein solah hain.' | 'जी, S4 में सोलह हैं।'

habits: DEVICE: a plain black smartphone in a plain black case, in his trouser pocket, charged every night at ten; normal text size, since his eyes are good. On the night train it dies by 10 pm because he has refreshed the running status since noon (the worry line's reason, shown plainly, never as an age joke).

SCRIPT: English in Latin letters for everything he types, in all three language modes, because that is how he types and because 'Reached?' marks no gender while 'पहुँच गए?' does (rule 66). Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages too.

SHAPE: he types the way he speaks. Each line is one short whole English sentence with its verb, a capital and a full stop, one fact to a line, in order. Times in figures with a colon (9:40, never 9.40 or 'nine forty').

NUMBERS: the speech budget carried onto the screen: at most one figure a line, and at least one line in three with none ('Charge your phone tonight.'). No prices, no scores, no numbered lists (no '1.', no ticks: Mami's), no ordinals.

THREE FIXED LINES, his only ones with no full sentence: 'Reached?' (after any journey you make without him; it means 'I missed you'; his alone in the cast), 'Noted.' (his reply when he has nothing to add), 'Good morning.' (under the 6:35 picture).

FULL STOPS: the family reads them as cross; they are not. The method notes cite NPR's report of a study where a one-word text ending in a full stop read as less sincere. The story can use the misreading once, with Tinku explaining it.
SPEED: one slow forefinger, the phone in his other palm; he rereads before sending; no typos; autocorrect off.

REPLIES: within a minute, always ('Noted.'), distinct from Mausa ji's 'Ok.' an hour later. Distinct too from Captain sahab's telegram style with no punctuation, Mummy's and Tinku's lowercase, and Mama ji's and Mausi's doubled marks.
EMOJI AND STICKERS: none. VOICE NOTES: never sends one (he says they have no time in them); he listens to Mausi's in full and replies in text.

FORWARDS: none, except one good-morning picture to the family at 6:35, after the walk with Captain sahab (a sunflower, or a glass of tea on a sunny windowsill; never a lotus, which is a party symbol, never a marigold, which leans to ritual, never a god or a famous face, rule 3) with 'Good morning.' under it. Never politics, never false news, never a forward he has not read.
CALLS: anything that matters is a call, made at the minute he said he would call. Nani gets calls, never texts.
TIMING: 'Reached?' goes out within ten minutes of your train's due time, by the running status, not the timetable.
ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' label, no group chat (owner, 23 Oct).
samples: TO YOU, MARCH, BOOKING DAY: 'The booking is done. / We have 12 berths. / They are on my railway pass and 2 PNRs.' then, a month later, on its own: 'Mausi has added 4 names. / No berths are left.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'बुकिंग हो गई। / हमारे पास 12 बर्थ हैं। / मेरे रेलवे पास और 2 PNR पर हैं।' then 'मौसी ने 4 नाम और जोड़े। / अब कोई बर्थ नहीं बची।' (who is on the pass is never said, rule 8; 'railway pass' because 'मेरे पास' alone also means 'with me')

TO YOU, THE NIGHT BEFORE: 'We are in coach S4. / Berth 36 is yours, a lower berth. / The train comes on platform 3. / It leaves at 9:40. / Carry your own water bottle. / Charge your phone tonight.' | Devanagari if wanted: 'हम कोच S4 में हैं। / बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है, नीचे की। / गाड़ी प्लेटफ़ॉर्म 3 पर आती है। / 9:40 पर छूटती है। / पानी की बोतल अपनी रखना। / आज रात बैटरी पूरी रखना।' (four lines with one figure, two with none; 36 is a real lower berth in the run 33 to 44, so Mausi keeps 33; the last line is the irony nobody remarks on: by ten that night his own phone is dead)
TO YOU, AFTER ANY JOURNEY WITHOUT HIM: 'Reached?' (one word, in English letters in every mode)
TO YOU, AFTER THE WARD NIGHT, 10:02 AM: 'Nani reached home at 10:00. / Sleep now.' | 'नानी 10:00 बजे घर पहुँच गईं। / अब सो लो।'
TO YOU, A WEEKDAY, WHEN YOU WILL BE HOME LATE (his one message with no number and nothing to arrange): 'The dal is on the stove.' | 'दाल गैस पर है।'
REPLY TO ANYTHING YOU SEND: 'Noted.' | 'दर्ज है।'

TO MAMI, DECEMBER: 'The guest train times are below. / The morning train is at 6:10. / The night train is at 9:40. / Both are confirmed. / I will meet both.' | 'मेहमानों की गाड़ियों का समय नीचे है। / सुबह की गाड़ी 6:10 पर है। / रात की गाड़ी 9:40 पर है। / दोनों कन्फ़र्म हैं। / दोनों पर मैं रहूँगा।' (she answers with her own list; his name heads her item 1 'Papa: trains', in her shape, not his)

THE FAMILY, EVERY MORNING (mentioned, never shown as a group; if a message is ever shown it is one message card with no group name, app look or 'forwarded' label): a picture of a sunflower at 6:35, then 'Good morning.'

changed: LENGTH (C2): from one sentence of four to ten words a beat, which put him among the eight clipped speakers, to an ordered run of whole sentences across one to three bubbles, each one fact, the last naming the next step. He is now one of the four long talkers, and his long shape (closed announcements in order) is unlike Mama ji's run-on, Mausi's triple and Masterji's wander.

NUMBERS (C1): kept as one of the two leaners, because the timetable is his essence, but budgeted at one figure a bubble and one bubble in three with none. The 1.08 line 'Sixteen of us have twelve berths. 9:40, not 9:45.' held four figures in one bubble; it is now three bubbles of one figure each. Five of his twelve test lines carry a figure. Prices, scores and ordinals are out of his speech and his card notes ('a fourth time' became 'again').

THE QUOTED LINE: '9:40, not 9:45.' became '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, not "around".' It keeps the correction and moves his quarrel to where his never list already put it (vague times), with one figure. Owner call: the old line was picked by the players' judge, so it may stay as one marked two-figure exception if the owner prefers it.

EXCLAMATION (C6): none before; now 'Kamaal hai.' | 'Remarkable.', said flat with a full stop, for real surprise and for dry irony. No religious sense. Mama ji's 'Kamaal!' goes so the word has one owner.

SORRY (C4): never in words before; now the record corrected against himself: '9:40 mera time tha. Galat nikla.' plus the right fact. Kept apart from Mausa ji's 'Galti hui.' (no subject, no time) and Mausi's 'sorry'.

THANKS (C4): before, only the praise 'It's confirmed.'; now the deed and its minute, then 'Darj hai.' (entered in the register), and the same word when he is thanked, followed by the next job. 'Darj' is Hindi and is the parcel register's word, so his English stays railway nouns and times only.

MIX (C12): 'Confirm ho gaya.' and 'note kar liya' were an English word plus ho or kar, the frame the matrix gives to Mummy alone. They became 'Sab confirm hai.' (the railway status) and 'Darj hai.'; his verbs are now Hindi railway verbs (gaadi lagna, chhootna, chalna, chart banna). When cross even 'late' and 'halt' go.

WORDS FROM (C11): beyond railway nouns, now his own past (his father the goods-train guard, the colony gate, the last coach, 'the 9:40 wali') and the dal he cooks by taste, his one interest with no number ('Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. Swaad se banti hai.'), as the comics review asked for Papa, Mummy and Mami.

FEELING (C3): still a deed and never a feeling word, but the deed is now spoken as something already done ahead ('Neeche ki berth aapki hai. March mein hi ho gayi thi.'), which tells him apart from Mausa ji's deed with his hands, now, and from Mummy's shop news. The colony-gate boy gets one spoken run, to Nani only, as facts with the feeling left under them; it is optional and never on the wordless 2:10 halt panel.

HOW ARE YOU (C10): he no longer dodges with a clock time; he answers with the state of everyone's trains ('Sab gaadiyan time par hain. Matlab main bhi.'), no figure, which also says what he wants: everyone arriving.

HUMOUR (C13): still deadpan about himself and clocks, now with a frame of its own, the station loudspeaker ('Kripya dhyan dein. Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.'), so his dry lines cannot be mistaken for Captain sahab's sardonic calls or your deadpan mirror. At most once a chapter, never while he asks, and all of it waits on rulebook Q5.

ONE OWNER PER WORD (matrix 2.15): dropped 'sharp' and 'theek' (worn out by three askers; 'Theek.' is Mausa ji's), 'pehle' and 'pehle se' (yours: 'Lower berth 33 is already yours' and 'Bag pehle upar' were rewritten), 'pakka', and 'Badi himmat hai' (the irony now rides on 'Kamaal hai.').

TALKS TO (C15): his longest runs go to Nani, who lets him finish; test lines are also said to Mama ji (the latecomer), the cousin, Tinku (the sugar), Captain sahab (the rumour) and a child, so he is heard with others, not only with you.

RULE 66: Hindi lines to you were reworded where it cost nothing ('बैटरी ख़त्म है' for 'ख़त्म हो गई', 'छूटने का समय 9:40 है' for a future), and the album's 'एक बार भी' became 'कभी'. The checker will still flag lines such as बुझेगी, जाएँगे, आएगा, छूटा, पड़ा, हुईं, चल पड़ी, यहीं हूँ and तुम्हारी है; each agrees with a thing, 'koi', an adverb or Papa himself, never with you, and a native reader clears them.

TYPING: one figure a line and at least one line in three with none (the old night-before message had 'Berths 33 to 44' and 'Platform 3. 9:40.' on single lines); each line a whole English sentence with its verb, the way he speaks; added the dal message, his one text with no number; your berth is 36, a real lower berth in the 33 to 44 run, so Mausi keeps 33; 'my railway pass' so the Hindi 'मेरे पास' cannot be read as 'with me'. 'Reached?', 'Noted.', the 6:35 sunflower, no emoji and no voice notes all stay.

KEPT AS THEY WERE: essence, want, fear and contradiction; 'Tonight, you are in charge.' at 1.10 with the list laid on the berth; the booking line at 1.04; the 6:10 birth joke; 'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.'; the Tamil count (now the one marked exception to one figure a bubble, a whisper to himself, once in chapter 1); the cross tell (minutes left, one word twice, the guard's flat hand); every address word and every rule-66 form to you.

voices.name: Mama ji (मामा जी), 47

voice.register: Fast, warm and run-on: a man walking between two building sites with his right arm up, talking to someone far away. His shape is the one run-on that grows: clauses chained with commas, 'aur haan' and 'aur ek', and no full stop till the last bubble, so a long thought takes two to four bubbles of at most ten words, each ending on a comma until the last ('Ek kaam karo, gate pe raho, aur haan,' / 'Bade Jija ji ko bulao, chairs bhi,' / 'sabko andar lo, sabko jagah. Pakka?'). It is the longest single sentence in the cast and it is told apart from the other long runs by its ending: Papa's are whole sentences with full stops, Masterji's a verdict and a wander, Mausi's a tripled word and a question she answers herself, and his is one sentence that never quite ends. His questions are worry checks about named people, stacked, and he waits only for the answer to the last one, 'Pakka?'; he never answers them himself. Feeling is said out loud, warmly, to one person at a time, with a hug: he is one of the two elders who say it in plain words (Mausi says hers to the whole room, loud; he says his to one face). Fear he says only to Mami. Humour is big and kind and aimed at himself (he plans nothing, he talks too much), never at anyone's age, town, shop or work. He talks most to people far away, Mummy first ('Didi!'); in chapter 5, with the phone in his pocket, to everyone at the gate. With Nani alone he slows to short whole sentences, the only person he slows for, and lets her finish before he speaks. When cross he does not go quiet or slow (that is Mami's tell in his chapter): the run-on stops dead and breaks into single words, one downward chop of his free hand on each ('Aaj. Abhi. Yahin.'), and even then he asks after the other man's family first. Never at family, a woman, a worker's dignity or anyone on a card. His voice is never raised except the chapter's one shout at 5.03 (rule 35). Warm, and never the comic one while he is the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: The most English elder. Hinglish: a whole English clause first, at speed, then a Hindi landing ('Don't worry, Bade Jija ji ko bulao, aur haan,'). The order and the cargo are his alone: his English leads and carries the jobs and the warmth (don't worry, no problem, sorted, extra, full, credit, department, I missed you, I'll miss you), and his Hindi lands on family, food and feeling (Amma, Didi, ghar, sab, khaana, dawai, man, roz). Mami, the other whole-clause switcher, runs the other way: a Hindi clause, then an English status ('pending', 'done', 'Correct?'). He never builds an English verb with kar or ho ('check karo', 'confirm karo', 'call karo'), because that frame is Mummy's alone: his English comes as whole clauses or bare nouns ('ticket bhi book?'). 'Ek kaam karo' to you, Tinku and Mami; 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders. Figures in Hinglish bubbles are digits ('60? 70 kar do!'), because romanised 'saath' is also 'with' (India review). HINDI MODE: everyday spoken city Hindi in Devanagari that keeps more English loan words than anyone else's (एक्स्ट्रा, फ़ुल, सेट, नो प्रॉब्लम, क्रेडिट, डिपार्टमेंट, प्रमोशन), so he still sorts in Hindi; 'चिंता मत करो' or 'चिंता नहीं' for 'don't worry' (never फ़िक्र, Masterji's word); with Nani, whole Hindi sentences and आप. ENGLISH MODE: plain British English with his rhythm, the trailing comma and 'oh, and' for 'aur haan'; 'Do one thing' at most once a chapter (his one Indian-English turn), otherwise 'One small job'; 'Oho!' stays; kin words stay as they are (Didi, Jija ji, Amma, Boss); never a spelled accent (caricature traps). With Nani in English mode the slowing carries the beat that Hindi mode carries with whole Hindi sentences.
tics: The run-on that grows: 'Ek kaam karo,' and the one thing grows ('aur haan,', 'aur ek,') until it is four; every bubble but the last ends on a comma. In English mode 'aur haan' is 'oh, and'.

Stacks worry questions about named people and waits only for the last answer: 'Amma ka BP? Dawai? Koi saath hai? Pakka?'. He never answers his own question (Mausi's shape) and never asks how you are (Nani's 'Aur tum.' closes that in the album).
Ends every worry stack and every reassurance he is given with 'Pakka?' ('Sure?'); at 5.27 it turns round into a statement.

People first, then business: every vendor gets 'Ghar mein sab theek?' and a question about their own people (a mother's knee, the children's exams) before 'Achha,' and the job. Names, not numbers, are his stock, and he keeps it even when cross.

Makes everything bigger in words, never in figures: aur, sab, sabko, extra, full ('full family', 'full kasoor', 'full fit'). The plus-ten is a gesture, the flashed open hand, with no figure said; the only spoken figures in his year are 5.03 and 5.27.
Hands the how to someone else in the same breath: 'Bade Jija ji ko bulao,', 'Credit Jija ji ka,'. He plans nothing; he knows who can.

Credits people out loud by their job, to whoever is near: 'In-charge se miliye!', 'Ghar ki railway se miliye!', and from December 'District scorer se miliye!' (outside any decision beat, guests off the panel).
'Oho!' for good or bad news, by tone; 'Achha,' as the hinge from the family question to the job; 'Aaiye' once at the gate, never three times (triples are Mausi's).
Never talks over Nani: he lets her finish, then repeats her last two words back.
Hugs everyone he can reach while he says it out loud (a stage direction, never a word). Never you: household hands never reach towards you (rule 7).
catchphrases: 'Ek kaam karo, ... aur haan,' | 'एक काम करो, ... और हाँ,' | 'Do one thing, ... oh, and,' The one thing that becomes four. 'Ek kaam kijiye' to vendors and elders; in English mode 'Do one thing' once a chapter, otherwise 'One small job,'. The 'ek' is an idiom, not a count.
'Pakka?' | 'पक्का?' | 'Sure?' The end of every worry stack, his word in the cast table. Turned round once, at 5.27: 'Pakka.' | 'पक्का।' | 'For sure.'

'60? 70 kar do!' | 'साठ? सत्तर कर दो!' | 'Sixty? Make it seventy!' His quoted line and his only catchphrase with a number, said once, at 5.03, the chapter's one shout, with the open hand flashed. The owner is asked whether to keep both marked figures (matrix open point).
voice.exclamation: 'Oho!' | 'ओहो!' | 'Oho!' (the same in every mode). For good news and bad, and the tone tells which: a rising 'Oho!' with the arm up when a job lands, a falling 'Oho.' with a hand to his forehead at a delay. It is a sound with no word in it, so it has no religious sense, and it is his alone in the cast (the India review and Mami's file both give it to him). Guard: never run on into a god-word, and never the city man's reflexes 'Thank God', 'Oh God', 'Oh my God', 'OMG', 'God bless', 'Shukar hai' or 'Bhagwan ka shukar' (rule 3). Never 'Kamaal!' (Papa's 'Kamaal hai.') and never any 'arre' (Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.').
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: blame, out loud and made bigger, the way he makes everything bigger: 'Didi, full kasoor mera. Full!' | 'दीदी, पूरा क़सूर मेरा। पूरा!' | 'Didi, it's all my fault. All of it!'. Said to whoever he let down, Mummy most of all, in front of everyone, and never with the English word 'sorry' (Mausi's alone). THANKS: public credit by job, loudly, to whoever is near, so the thank-you is the room hearing what you did: 'In-charge se miliye!' | 'इंचार्ज से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the in-charge!'; for Papa 'Ghar ki railway se miliye!' | 'घर की रेलवे से मिलिए!' | 'Meet the family's railway!'. Thanked himself, he gives the credit away to whoever did the how: 'Not me! Credit Jija ji ka.' He never says 'thank you' or 'shukriya' (Mami's to strangers, and yours). LOVE: said in plain words, one to one, with a hug: 'Amma, I missed you. Roz.' | 'अम्मा, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगा। रोज़।' | 'Amma, I missed you. Every day.'; at a parting 'Didi, I'll miss you.' | 'दीदी, आपके बिना मन नहीं लगेगा।' and the worry stack after it; to Mami in private, what she did, said back to her ('aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha.'). Never 'bahut yaad' or 'याद आई' (Mausi's). FEAR: only to Mami ('Main wahan nahi tha, Boss. Phir se.').

habits: Device: a big plain black phone in a thick black rubber case with one corner cracked on a site, painted with the screen dark and no logo, every word live text laid on top (rule 30). In chapter 5 it stays in his trouser pocket: never painted, never typed on screen.
Script: English and Roman Hinglish, never Devanagari (Nani's voice-typed Devanagari is the contrast). In the game's Hindi mode his messages show in Devanagari and keep his bursts and marks.
Shape: the run-on typed as a burst. Four or five short messages, each one clause of it, 'aur haan' a message of its own, then 'calling' before you can reply.

The first message is the person's name, capitalised, with his doubled mark ('Didi!!', 'Jija ji!!', 'In-charge!!'); everything after it is lowercase, kin names included ('amma', 'nani', 'chhote'), with no full stops. To Mami in private the name comes with no mark at all ('Boss').
Marks: '!!' is his; a worry question takes one '?', because '??' is Mausi's; never '!!!'.

Numbers: his bigness is typed in words (sab, everyone, extra, full), never as figures and never as the plus-ten. A digit appears only when a fact someone must act on cannot be said another way, and then he would rather ring.

Emoji: 🎉 for good news, ‼️ for worry, and 🤗 (a face with no person, gender or skin tone) for love typed in words ('miss you all 🤗'): he is the only one in the family who types love. 💯 is retired: it was a number sign and his old number habit. Never a person emoji; no folded hands until the owner rules (realism notes).
Capitals once a year, for joy (Tinku's course letter), never in anger: all caps reads as shouting, the 'aggro uncle' trap (realism notes).

Voice notes from the back of an auto between sites, starting mid-word because he presses record late; shown as a voice-note strip with their words as live text, and they run on like his speech ('...aur haan, aur ek,').

Forwards: only weather warnings for Nani's district, each with one line of his own ('amma ko andar rakhiye na!!'), the warning painted blank. Never politics, religion, gods, famous faces or false news (rule 3; caricature traps).

When: just before his eight o'clock call to Nani, at red lights, and late at night after Mami's list. He replies in seconds or not at all, because he rings instead, and never reads a long message to the end ('ok ok call me').
Short forms: 'pls', 'ok ok', 'msg'. No spelled accent and no typo played for laughs. No English verb with kar ('call karo' became 'call me'), since that frame is Mummy's.
In private with Mami, and only there, his asks come down, in words: 'sabko?' becomes 'ok sab nahi' becomes 'tumhari list'.
The game has no group chat (owner, 23 Oct). On screen he is single messages on a painted blank phone or a message card under a panel, and a message on the player's own phone waits on rulebook Q9.

changed: NUMBERS (C1): every spoken figure struck except the two marked beats, 5.03 '60? 70 kar do!' and 5.27 '60 plates. Pakka.'. The plus-ten stays only as the flashed open hand. His bigness moves into words (aur, sab, sabko, extra, full). The joke '60 kursiyaan? 10 log khade-khade.' became 'Kursiyaan kam padin toh log khade-khade, khaana jaldi niptega,'; the temper line's 'do din se' became 'kal bhi... parson bhi'.

NUMBERS IN TYPING (C1, typing pass): '2 tickets 14th night' to Papa became 'tomorrow night / me and Boss'; 'tent coming 4 pm' to you became 'tent aaj shaam'; the private 'boss 70 final? / ok 65 / ok ok 60' to Mami became 'sabko bulayein? / ok sab nahi / ok ok tumhari list', so his asks still come down in private, now in words and towards her list; 💯 retired, because it was a number sign.
'KAMAAL!' STRUCK from the Papa tease, now 'Oho!' (matrix 2.15: 'Kamaal hai.' is Papa's new exclamation). 'Oho!' stays his one exclamation, secular, a sound with no word in it.

LOVE LINE (C16): Hinglish 'Amma, I missed you. Bahut.' became 'Roz.', English 'So much.' became 'Every day.', so 'bahut yaad' stays Mausi's alone; his Hindi 'आपके बिना मन नहीं लगा।' already differed and gains 'रोज़।'. Love is now said out loud to more than Nani: 'Didi, I'll miss you.' at a parting, and what Mami did said back to her in private.

SORRY AND THANKS SET (C4: he had neither): sorry is blame made bigger, 'Didi, full kasoor mera. Full!'; thanks is public credit by job, and when he is thanked he gives the credit away ('Not me! Credit Jija ji ka.'). Neither is a deed, and neither uses 'sorry' (Mausi's), 'thank you' (Mami's) or 'shukriya' (yours).

'NO TENSION' STRUCK: Mausi's target gives 'tension' to her English. His reassurance is 'Don't worry' (the realism notes' own example for him, and Mummy's, Papa's and Mausa ji's files already call it his); in Hindi mode 'चिंता मत करो' / 'चिंता नहीं', never फ़िक्र, which is Masterji's.

THE RUN-ON MADE VISIBLE (C2): every bubble but the last ends on a comma, 'aur haan' gets a fixed English form ('oh, and'), and each test line shows the trailing comma inside its one bubble, so his long shape survives the 10-word cap (rule 62) and reads apart from Papa's full stops, Masterji's wander and Mausi's triple.

ENGLISH VERB + KAR STRUCK: 'ok ok call karo' became 'ok ok call me'; the never list now bars 'check karo', 'confirm karo', 'book karo', because the matrix gives that frame to Mummy alone. His English comes as whole clauses, which is what keeps his mix apart from Mummy's.

MIX SPLIT FROM MAMI (C12 near-miss): both switch whole clauses, so the order and the cargo now differ: his English leads and carries jobs and warmth, then Hindi lands on family; hers is a Hindi clause, then an English status.

HINDI MODE KEPT SORTABLE: he keeps more English loan words in Devanagari than anyone (एक्स्ट्रा, फ़ुल, सेट, नो प्रॉब्लम, क्रेडिट, डिपार्टमेंट), because the blind test runs again in Hindi and a voice that sorts only in Hinglish fails two of three modes.
ENGLISH MODE: 'Do one thing' at most once a chapter, otherwise 'One small job', so his one Indian-English turn stays one turn.

TEA TAKEN OUT OF HIS CARE (C3: tea carried four people's care): 'Boss, chai. List kal.' became 'Boss, list band karo, kal subah, aur haan,' / 'aaj poora ghar tumne sambhala. Maine dekha.', love said in words, and the old clipped two-word shape (C2) gone; at the gate 'sabko chai' became 'sabko jagah'.
JOKE AT HIMSELF ADDED: 'Plan Boss ka department hai,' / 'mera department sirf log, aur haan,'. The target asks for humour big, kind and at himself, and the old jokes were about the crowd.

POLITE FORMS FIXED: 'In-charge se milo!' became 'miliye!' (guests are elders and strangers); vendors get 'Ek kaam kijiye' to match his own address rule, 'आप to all'; forwards to Didi say 'rakhiye na', the आप softened with 'na' that his address rule for her asks.
'POORI GALI' NOT USED: Nani's new voice owns 'मेरी पूरी गली।', so his lane is 'gali mein sabko'.

TYPING MARKS: the opener is the listener's name with '!!' and the rest lowercase, one consistent rule where the old samples mixed cases; 'DISTRICT LEVEL!!!' became '!!' (doubled is his mark, triples are Mausi's shape); 'r u at nani's' (whose Hindi 'यहाँ हो' trips the rule 66 checker) is gone; love is now typed in words with 🤗, the one family member who types it.

OWNERSHIP GUARDS ADDED to the never list: 'Pehle ___' (yours), any 'arre' (Captain sahab's), 'first class' and every ordinal, 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' (Mausa ji's), 'Badhaai ho' beside 'Main hoon na' as famous titles, and 'Thank God' and its kin named outright, since a city man reaches for them first.

C10 FIXED FOR HIM: asked how he is, he answers 'Full fit!' and turns straight to everyone else's medicines, with no figure and no trade dodge, which keeps his want (worried about everyone but himself) on the page.
C15: in the test set he speaks to the tent man, Papa, Mummy, a neighbour and a child, not only to you, so he is heard with the others.

KEPT, unchanged in substance: his essence, want, fear and contradiction (worries about everything, plans nothing; makes anyone come); 'Pakka?' and its turn at 5.27; 'Ek kaam karo'; the stacked worry questions he never answers himself; people before business; the cross tell (the run-on breaking into single words with a chop of the hand); slowing down only for Nani; fear said only to Mami; the address table.

OPEN, for the owner and readers: keep both marked figures (5.03 and 5.27)? A Hindi-first reader checks 'घर की रेलवे' (the gender of रेलवे), 'फ़ुल फ़िट', 'नो प्रॉब्लम' and 'क्रेडिट' in Hindi mode, and 'Kursiyaan kam padin'; 🤗 is proposed as his and no other file claims it; every joke still waits on rulebook Q5.

voices.name: Tinku (टिंकू), 21

voice.register: Quick, light and teasing: the fastest young voice in the house. Two sentence shapes, both hers alone. (1) The scoreline: the result as a score or a tally, then her tag 'haan?' to soften a tease ('3-0, haan?', 'Ye 4, Mami.', '3 mein 0.'). (2) The commentary aside: something that has just happened, called live in the present tense, the way the commentator she wanted to be at nine would call it ('Aur ye gaya!', 'Kya debut!', 'Seedhe kitaab mein.'). Lines run two to six words, one bubble, said fast. In chapter 4 her questions are the decisions themselves, asked plainly with no tag (rule 37), crisp and warm, never the comic one. To Nani she slows into whole, careful, polite Hindi sentences with -इए and no tag. Moved, she goes very short and plain, with no figure and no tag ('March. Jawaab: haan.'). Cross, she gets faster but not louder (Mausi is the one who gets louder): flat and exact, she reads out the whole record in two or three chained bubbles, then the book snaps shut and the ear cups go on. She talks most to you, as an equal and a rival; then to Nani, in polite Hindi.
voice.mix: Young small-town Hinglish: a Hindi frame carrying English nouns from the scorebook and the commentary box (run, over, wicket, total, tally, extras, score, record, final, keeper, boundary, replay, debut, match, innings) and one tag, 'haan?', which she keeps in all three modes. Commerce words (stock, bill, balance, accounts, hisaab, profit) leave her speech, so the shop family's talk does not tip into the trader idiom (india review); 'tally' and 'total' stay because a scorer uses them. No whole English clauses at home: whole-clause switching belongs to Mama ji and Mami. Her English shows more in her typing than in her speech. With Nani: plain polite Hindi, आप, every word in full, no English except Nani's own nouns (doctor, BP) and 'scorer', Nani's word for her; the one marked exception is '80, not out, Nani.' at the homecoming. With Mummy, Papa and the other elders: the same Hindi frame with आप and ji; her teasing rides on numbers, so it never needs a familiar 'you' to an elder. With you: तुम, only in commands, 'who should' questions and lines where you are not the doer (rule 66). Hindi mode: the cricket nouns stay as everyday loans in Devanagari (रन, विकेट, स्कोर, बाउंड्री, रिप्ले), and she says तीन-ज़ीरो, not the formal तीन-शून्य (Hindi-first readers confirm). Hinglish mode: every number is a figure ('3-0', '3 mein 0'), so a number is never misread as a word. English mode: plain young English with cricket idiom, numbers as words, 'haan?' kept.
tics: The scoreline: gives the result as a score or a tally, never an ordinal: '3-0.' | 'तीन-ज़ीरो।' | 'Three-nil.'; '3 mein 0.' | 'तीन में ज़ीरो।' | 'Nil out of three.' ('Teesri baar' becomes '3 baar': ordinals leave every speaker, matrix 2.15.)
Ends a tease with 'haan?' | 'हाँ?', in every mode. Never 'hai na?' (Mausi's), 'Correct?' or 'Sahi?' (Mami's) or 'Pakka?' (Mama ji's).

The commentary aside (new): calls a small household moment live, in the present tense, like a commentator: 'Aur ye gaya!' | 'और ये गया!' | 'And that's gone!'; 'Kya entry!' | 'क्या एंट्री!' | 'What an entry!'. It is her shape with no number in it.
Keeps a running tally of people's habits, out loud, to their face: 'Ye 4, Mami.' | 'ये चार, मामी।' | 'That's four, Mami.'
Says 'Kitaab mein.' when anyone makes a promise: it is written down now.

NEW SHAPE WITH NO NUMBER: the commentary aside ('Aur ye gaya!', 'Kya debut!', 'Kya entry!'), from the commentator she wanted to be at nine (Mausi's relationship note). Why: C2 and C11; she was told apart only by figures and scoring nouns, and now has a sentence shape of her own.
NEW EXCLAMATION: 'Gazab!' | 'ग़ज़ब!' | 'Brilliant!' (C6: she had none), with a guard against 'ख़ुदा का ग़ज़ब' and a fallback, 'Zabardast!'.

SORRY AND THANKS SET (C4: she had neither): sorry 'Mera wicket.', thanks 'Run tumhara.' / 'Run aapka.'. When she is thanked she hands the run back, which also keeps her contradiction: the credit never goes in her own column.

'NOT OUT' ONLY AFTER A TOTAL: '80, not out, Nani.' stays as her love line. 'Shutter up at nine. Not out, Mummy.' becomes 'Mummy, aapke 42, mere 42. Match tie.' Why: C7, Captain sahab keeps the bare call; the new line also pays off the flood argument in which both counts are right. 'Not out.' leaves her catchphrases. 'Match tie', not 'barabar', because 'Barabar.' is Masterji's verdict in his new file.
CATCHPHRASES are now 'Kitaab mein.', '3-0, haan?' and 'Faisla tumhara.'; only one carries a number.

COMMERCE WORDS OUT: stock, bill, accounts and hisaab leave her speech and typing; 'tally' and 'total' stay as scorer's words. Why: the india review's trader-idiom point (C11). Her words now come from play.

DROPPED TIC 'repeats a number back as a check (Fourteen? Fourteen.)'. Why: head-counts in speech are Nani's, once (matrix 2.15), and a readback is Mami's shape. For the same reason chapter 1's 'Counted twice, Papa.' becomes 'Sab andar, Papa. Over poora.'; 'counts twice' was also one of the trading phrases the india review named.

CROSS TELL SHARPENED: faster and flatter, never louder (Mausi is the one who gets louder), written as two or three chained bubbles of at most 10 words (rule 62). The record is now a tally of what the person did ('"sabse chhoti": 12 baar', 'vaade: 3 mein 0'), not the old 'March, nil. May, nil.' items, which read like Mami's 'thing, status' list.

THE DODGE (her contradiction) is kept but always aims at a named person's tally, never a clock or a price, so it no longer shares C10's figure key with Papa's times and Mummy's prices: 'Mere marks, Mausi? Mausa ji ne aaj 9 baar "Hmm" kaha.'

MIX: her English tags fold into one, 'haan?', kept in all three modes so that she can be sorted in English and Hindi as well as Hinglish; no whole English clauses at home (Mama ji's and Mami's pattern).

WORDS STRUCK because someone else owns them: 'done' in her typing (Mami's status word). Her never-list now names every owned word from matrix 2.15 and the targets ('pakka', 'Sahi?', 'arre', 'Lo', 'Theek', 'Galti', 'Pehle', English 'sorry' and the rest). The sibling files already written (Nani, Mummy, Mausi, Mausa ji, Masterji) list 'Gazab' and 'haan?' as hers, and none uses her new words.

TYPING: to elders 'aap' and 'aapne' instead of 'u'; Nani's message says 'सुबह वाली दवाई' instead of 'आठ बजे वाली'; Captain sahab's message loses '9 baje'; Mummy's flood message loses 'shutter 9 baje?' and ends on 'match tie'; her exclamation and her commentary type as 'gazabbb' and 'aur ye gayaaa'.

RULE 66: every Hindi line to you is a command, a 'who should' question, verbless, or a line where you are not the doer. Lines the checker flags and a native reader clears: फ़ैसला तुम्हारा, रन तुम्हारा and गिनती मेरी (each agrees with its noun), कौन देखे? (the rulebook's own cleared kind), पापा ... टोक चुके (Papa is the doer) and मैं ख़ुद लिखूँगी (Tinku is the doer).

KEPT AS THEY WERE: essence, want, fear and contradiction; तुम to you and आप to every elder; whole polite Hindi to Nani; 'Pick three, one a keeper. Fast, haan?'; 'Two targets. Today, your call.'; 'Ji nahin, Mami ... 10 season se.'; 'Baitho. Aaj raat ginti meri.'; 'In the book.'; 'Your one trial again, Captain sahab?'; and the rule that she never doubts a report.

KNOCK-ON FOR HER CAST FILE: year_arc and best_scenes need chapter 1's line ('Sab andar, Papa. Over poora.'), chapter 2's 8 am message card (doses by meal, 'सुबह, दोपहर, रात', not clock times), chapter 3's shutter line ('Match tie') and the essence's quoted line updated. Captain sahab's file keeps the bare 'Not out.'

FOR THE READERS: 'Gazab' (a Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader), 'oye' to you (kept, rare), '80, not out, Nani' as the one English phrase she says to Nani, and तुम to you (Hindi-first readers, as before).

voices.name: Mausi (मौसी), about 55, chapter 1 voice

voice.register: Hindi-first; the loudest and fastest voice in the cast, warm and bossy like a front-room tuition teacher talking to Class 3. She talks in bursts: two to four bubbles of short closed sentences, every one ending on ! or ?, the first bubble starting over the end of yours. The shape is hers alone: a tripled first word, a question she answers herself, 'hai na?', and she has moved on before anyone can reply. Her long run is a string of short loud sentences, never a comma chain (Mama ji's run-on) and never a list (Mummy's jobs, Mami's statuses). Pace quick and rising. When cross she gets louder and faster, the only one in the family who does; when moved she goes silent, the only time she does. No numbers at all, not even ordinals. One shout bubble a chapter at most (rule 35, which is 1.09), and never a whisper, because she cannot whisper. Each bubble is at most 10 words (rule 62): a triple spends three of them, so the rest of that bubble stays short, and a longer thought becomes more bubbles. She is never the asker (rule 37) and never reacts to who was picked (rule 39).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame with single English words in it, the older speakers' pattern in the realism notes (1.1). What her English carries is feeling and school, not trade: sorry, tension, first class, topper, homework, copy (exercise book), class, teacher, fail, late mark; in chapter 1 also the travel nouns berth and chart. She never uses the English verb + kar/ho frame, which is Mummy's alone now (so no 'adjust karo', 'share karo', 'late ho gaye'), never a whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's way), and never 'thank you'. Her Hindi is everyday small-town Hindi with a teacher's words in it (inaam, bujho, copiyan, 'khaali pet'), never spelled to sound funny. Fillers that mark no region or faith: suno, chalo, accha, haan; no 'arre' (Captain sahab's), no 'dekho' and no 'Dekhiye' (Masterji's). The tag 'hai na?' is hers; in English mode it becomes a real tag question ('didn't I?', 'aren't you?', 'doesn't she?'), which nobody else in the cast uses. In Hinglish mode she reads as Roman Hindi with those English words (how a Hinglish bubble looks waits on rulebook Q6). A Hindi-first reader reads every line aloud (rule 65).
tics: Says her first word three times, once a run, at the start of its first bubble: 'Suno, suno, suno!' to call the room, 'Chalo, chalo, chalo!' to hurry it, 'Na, na, na!' to refuse, 'Sorry, sorry, sorry!' to apologise, 'Aao, aao, aao.' to comfort (her one soft triple, with full stops), or a name three times ('Munna, Munna, Munna!', 'Bhabhi, Bhabhi, Bhabhi!', 'Aji, aji, aji!'). Never 'arre' (Captain sahab's), and never 'haaye' tripled or doubled, because हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant.

Asks a question and answers it herself, like the riddle-setter she is every morning, blurting the answer before anyone can guess: 'Kiski? Hamari!', 'Main padosan hoon? Nahin!', 'Andhera? Koi baat nahin!'. The one question in the year she cannot answer herself is 'Kisne karwaayi?' at the lower berth, and then she goes silent.
Ends a statement with 'hai na?' and is gone before anyone answers; in English mode, a tag question.
Quotes people back word for word: 'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…'. Her memory is exact; she never misquotes.
Says what she feels, out loud, to the whole room: love ('Bahut yaad aayi'), hurt ('Amma pehle Chhoti ko bulaati hain!'), sorry. Silent only when moved, palm to her chest.

Runs the room like her class: marks the late ('Late mark!'), grades a favour ('Ekdum first class!'), fails herself when she is wrong ('Aaj teacher fail!'), and measures disasters by her pupils ('Copiyan upar!', 'meri class ka inaam'). This is what keeps her from being only the loud aunt who feeds: her teaching is in her mouth, not only in one wordless picture.

Food as punctuation: 'Pehle khao' (the only 'Pehle' that is hers; 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy is yours), 'Khaali pet baat nahin!', 'Muh meetha karo!', and something held out as she says it, her face in the frame.
Report-card verdicts on habits, never on character, in all her judging notes ('Never sits still for long.').
'Hamara, hamari' (ours) for anyone she is proud of ('hamari topper'), but never of you, since it would mark your gender.
When cross: louder and faster, hand on hip, the basket bag set down hard, and her own catchphrase fails ('Koi sunta bhi hai? Nahin!').
catchphrases: 'Suno, suno, suno!' | 'सुनो, सुनो, सुनो!' | 'Listen, listen, listen!' (her opener and the line people quote back; the tripled 'suno' is hers alone, so Tinku keeps 'oye' and she calls Mausa ji 'Aji')
'Maine kaha tha na?' | 'मैंने कहा था न?' | 'Didn't I say so?' (whenever something she predicted comes true, good news above all)

'Pichhle saal tumne kaha tha…' | 'पिछले साल तुमने कहा था…' | 'Last year you said…' (the quote-back; gender-free, because with तुमने the verb agrees with what was said; rule 66's checker flags कहा था and a native reader clears it). None of the three has a number in it.
voice.exclamation: 'Haaye!' | 'हाय!' | English mode 'Oh!'. For sympathy, surprise and delight, and just before she says a feeling ('Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.'). Nobody else in the cast uses it. It has no religious meaning on its own; the guard is that it is never followed by a name or a word for god or mother: no 'Hai Ram', 'Haaye Ram', 'Haaye Rabba', 'Haaye Allah', 'Haaye Maa', 'Ui Maa'. Never doubled or tripled (हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant). The English 'Oh!' avoids every hidden holy word on the 2.13 list (Gosh, Goodness, Oh my, Heavens). Open point for the English blind sort: if 'Oh!' gets mixed up with Mama ji's 'Oho!', keep 'Haaye!' in English mode too, as Mami keeps 'Ish'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: 'Sorry, sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.' | 'सॉरी, सॉरी, सॉरी! पहले खाओ।' | 'Sorry, sorry, sorry! Eat first.' The English word 'sorry' is hers alone in the cast; food is held out as she says it, her face in the frame. To an elder: 'Pehle khaiye.' THANKS: a teacher's grade, out loud, to the whole room: 'Ekdum first class!' | 'एकदम फ़र्स्ट क्लास!' | 'Absolutely first class!' Never 'thank you' (Mami's, to strangers) and never 'shukriya' (yours). WHEN SHE IS THANKED: she wants it heard: 'Haaye! Zor se kaho! Amma bhi sunein!' | 'हाय! ज़ोर से कहो! अम्मा भी सुनें!' | 'Oh! Say it louder! Let Amma hear too!' Only Amma's thanks, in December, makes her silent. LOVE: said out loud, to the whole room: 'Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.' | 'हाय! बहुत याद आई।' | 'Oh! I missed you so much.' At a parting, the same key: 'Abhi se yaad aa rahi!' | 'अभी से याद आ रही!' | 'Missing you already!' 'Bahut yaad' is hers alone (Mama ji now says 'Roz.'); his love is warm and one to one with a hug, hers is loud and to the room with food.

never: Any doubt of a report of being followed or harassed, or of a dowry demand: no 'sach mein?', 'pakka?', 'galatfehmi', 'misunderstanding', 'imagined', 'chhodo', 'jaane do', 'hota rehta hai' about it. She is the first to believe, and the hard topic never reaches a bubble or a story panel anyway (rule 26); she has no line in the lead-in or settle of a hard decision. Her 'Na, na, na!' and 'Kabhi nahin!' are for harmless news only.

Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Haaye Ram, Haaye Rabba, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar, Jesus, tauba, 'shukr hai', 'Ui Maa', 'Mata ji' as a goddess; in English mode no Gosh, Golly, Goodness, Oh my, Heavens, Lord, Thank God. No caste word, no brand.
Any number in speech: no figures, no counts, no years (rule 2), no ordinals ('teesri class' is struck), no 'ek-ek', 'teen baar' or 'sau mein sau'. 'First class' stays as an idiom of praise.

Any word that gives you a gender: beta, bachcha, bhaiya, didi, raja, rani; 'hamara/hamari' of you; any verb or adjective that agrees with you: kitne/kitni bade/badi ho gaye, aa gaye/aa gayi, thak gaye/gayi, -oge/-ogi (rules 8 and 66). 'How grown up you've got' becomes 'Chehre pe thakaan.'

Other people's words, so the blind sort can tell her apart: 'arre' (Captain sahab's 'Arre waah'), 'Ek-ek karke' and 'Pehle ___' as a courtesy (yours; she keeps only 'Pehle khao'), 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' (Mausa ji's), 'aur haan', 'Oho!', 'full', 'extra' and 'Roz' (Mama ji's), 'Kamaal' and 'Reached?' (Papa's), 'Had hai!', 'bill' and 'hisaab' (Mummy's), 'Gazab!' and the 'haan?' tag (Tinku's), 'Not out', 'Next ball', 'Well played' (Captain sahab's), 'Baap re', 'Bas', 'Chai piyo', 'Main yahin hoon' (Nani's), 'Uff', 'Dekhiye', 'mausam', 'barsaat' (Masterji's), 'Hain?', 'Mazboot', 'Galti hui', 'Ho jayega' (Mausa ji's), 'Ish', 'Tick', 'Correct?', 'pending' (Mami's), 'Badhiya', 'Shukriya', 'Maaf kijiye' (yours), 'pakka' (several files), 'Everyone comes'.
The English verb + kar/ho frame (Mummy's alone): no 'adjust karo', 'share karo', 'late ho gaye'. No whole English clause; no 'thank you'; no 'please' to family; no 'pata nahin' (she always knows).
A comma chain or a list: her long run is short closed sentences, never Mama ji's run-on or Mummy's and Mami's lists.

Character words or verdicts on anyone: aalsi, kaamchor, raub, besharam, badchalan, chalu; nothing on anyone's morals, marriage or dress; no sentence about ladkiyan, ladke, aurtein or mard in general (rule 22). Her talk is energy and care, never gossip about people.
The stock aunty's questions to you: shaadi, rishta (a match), salary or 'kitna kamate', weight, looks, skin colour (gori, kaali, saanwli) for anyone, 'naukri kab'.
A joke at her own body or age, or at her loudness as mockery: she laughs first and the strip laughs with her ('Meri class aise hi sunti hai'), never at her.
Film lines or famous catchphrases (rule 3): never 'Main hoon na'.
A second shout in a chapter; any whisper (rule 35).

Any card person's name, or any word from a decision's card notes, in a bubble before or during that decision, in either language (rule 36). In chapter 1 that rules out, until the decision that carries them: phone, tea, water, blanket, trip, 'last', bag, sari, tiffin, food (खाना), coach (डिब्बा), seat, window, family, everyone (सबके), पास, साथ, बार, तरह, joke, bus (and बस), platform, town (शहर), maths, coaching, teaches, and बोल. The test-set lines below are not panel lines; any line placed in a panel re-runs the build's note-word check.
address: To you: तुम, only in commands ('Ab batao', 'Idhar baitho', 'Pehle khao'), 'who should' asks, and lines where you are not the doer ('Chehre pe thakaan', 'Bahut yaad aayi', 'Tumhari khabar'); no address word, or her opening 'Suno, suno, suno!'. Never beta (rulebook Q7 is open, and it stays out until then), bachcha, bhaiya, didi. Lines rule 66's checker flags but a native reader clears: आई (agrees with याद), खाया (with कुछ), कहा था (with what was said), रखे (with पराठे).
To Nani: 'Amma', आप and -इए ('Amma, bujhiye kaun?', 'Pehle khaiye'). Never 'Ammi' (leans towards one community; realism 1.3).
To Mummy: 'Chhoti', तुम. In English mode, 'your Mummy' when she speaks of her to you.
To Papa: no address word, आप; to you, 'tumhare Papa'. Never 'Tinku ke Papa' (a wife's way of naming her own husband).
To Mama ji: 'Munna', तुम (his childhood pet name; readers confirm).
To Tinku: 'Tinku' or 'hamari topper', तुम.
To Mausa ji: 'Aji' | 'अजी', तुम both ways (he uses no word for her).
To Mami: 'Bhabhi', तुम.
To Masterji and Captain sahab: their titles and आप.
To strangers: 'Bhaiya' to the stall man, 'Sahab' to the ticket checker, आप; neither is ever a card person.

What they call her: Nani 'Badi' (तुम); Mummy and Papa 'Didi' (आप); Mama ji and Mami 'Badi Didi' (आप); Tinku and you 'Mausi' (आप, with -इए); Mausa ji no word ('tumhari Mausi' to you); Masterji 'Behenji'; Captain sahab and her old pupils 'Madam ji'. All for readers to confirm (rule 65), in the one family address table.

Bahut yaad aayi.' | Hindi 'हाय! बहुत याद आई।' (gender-free: आई agrees with याद; rule 66 check 3 flags it at the sentence end and a native reader clears it; 'bahut yaad' is hers alone now)

Why?' / 'A neighbour? Me? No! Now tell me, straight.' | Hinglish 'Suno, suno, suno! Tumhari khabar Chhoti se kyon?' / 'Main padosan hoon? Nahin! Ab batao. Hai na?' | Hindi 'अम्मा पहले छोटी को बुलाती हैं! है न?' ('hai na?' invites a denial nobody gives; 'pehle' here is a complaint, not your 'Pehle ___' courtesy)

habits: Device: a big-screen Android phone in a plain flip case with no markings (rule 3). She reads it held a hand's width from her nose, since she is short-sighted and wears no glasses; that distance is her phone trait (six files share 'font at its largest', so it is not). Painted blank; every word on it is live text (rule 30).

Mostly voice notes, long ones, the phone held flat under her chin like a plate and spoken at full volume so the whole room hears. They open 'Haan suno....' and close '....chalo, khana kha lena 😊' (the old close 'aur haan' is Mama ji's joiner now). On screen a voice note is a live-text card: a play mark, a long bar and her first words, with no length figure, so no number reaches her lines.
When she types: Roman Hinglish, all lowercase except 'OK', spelled the way she says it and always in full, never short forms like 'h' or 'k' (Masterji's and Tinku's).

Punctuation: four dots '....' between every phrase instead of full stops or commas; double question marks '??', which are hers (Mama ji keeps '!!'). One long message, never a burst of short ones (Mama ji's), never one item a line (Papa's), never a list (Mami's). She types her triple too, with no commas ('jaldi jaldi jaldi'), and her self-answered question ('kaun jeeta?? hamari topper').
No figures, even typed: no times, no counts, no prices. Her daily send is a riddle, not a sum.

Emoji: 😊 at the end of nearly everything, even bad news (the family knows to read past it); 😋 for food. Never 👍 (Mummy's), never a person emoji (it carries a gender and a skin tone), and 🙏 not at all until the owner decides (realism 2.2); she has no typed thank-you to put it after anyway.

Her one daily send is her own: 'aaj ki paheli' (today's riddle), a traditional children's riddle in words to the family group early each morning, whose answers she marks by voice note at night. Never a good-morning flower (Papa's), never gods, politics, a famous face, false news or a home remedy (rule 3; realism 2.2).
Timing: replies within seconds all day, answers a one-word message with a long voice note, and is sending from four in the morning. No reply means she is cooking.
Typos: autocorrect turns her Hinglish into English words and she sends it anyway; it is never shown as a joke on her.
The family group is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct). A message reaches the player as one message card.

How others' typing meets hers: Mummy answers 'ok 👍' within a minute in shop hours and never after nine; Papa replies with one full-stopped sentence; Tinku replies 'mausi 😂'; Mausa ji sits beside her and does not need to.
samples: To you, the evening before the train (a message card on the painted blank phone): 'suno suno suno....kal raat wali train....tum bhi saath ho na?? apni baatein seedha mujhe batana....chhoti se nahi 😊' (listen listen listen....tomorrow night's train....you're with us, aren't you?? tell me your news yourself....not through Chhoti). Gender-free: 'saath ho' and a command. If it is shown in chapter 1 it is a sign, so the note-word check applies (साथ).
To you, after any trip: 'khana khaya?? kya kya khaya?? 😋' (eaten?? what did you eat??). About food only: 'Reached?' is Papa's. Gender-free: खाया follows खाना.
Voice note to you before dawn, a live-text card: '▶ Haan suno.... neend nahi aayi....toh socha....' (Yes, listen.... couldn't sleep....so I thought....). No length figure on the card.

Family group, early morning (mentioned, or shown as a single card): 'aaj ki paheli....ek thaal moti se bhara, sabke sir par aundha dhara....kya hai?? jawab shaam tak....tinku tum mat batana 😊' (today's riddle....a plate full of pearls, held upside down over everyone's head....what is it?? answers by evening....Tinku, don't you answer). The answer is the night sky; a traditional children's riddle (readers confirm), where 'ek' is the article 'a', not a count.
To Mausa ji at night: 'aji....bp ki goli....abhi abhi abhi 😊' (aji....your BP pill....now now now)

To Mummy before dawn on the ward night, from Nani's house: 'chhoti....amma se baat hui....unko bhi neend nahi....subah aati hoon....tum so jao 😊' (Chhoti....spoke to Amma....she can't sleep either....I'll come in the morning....you go to sleep). Mummy, who never messages after nine, reads it in the morning.

To you, after your good news: 'haaye....maine kaha tha na?? ekdum first class....mithai kab?? 😋' (oh....didn't I say so?? absolutely first class....when are the sweets??). Gender-free: no verb agrees with you.

To Mummy, her hurt typed and then smiled over: 'amma ne aaj bhi pehle tumhe bulaaya....koi baat nahi....main toh hoon hi 😊' (Amma called you first again today....never mind....I'm always here anyway). The 😊 is why nobody hears it.

changed: Rhythm pinned against Mama ji, the other long talker: her long run is now a burst of short closed sentences, each ending on ! or ?, in two to four bubbles, never a comma chain or 'aur haan' (his run-on) and never a list (Mummy's, Mami's). Why: the matrix gives both plain feelers long runs, so the shape has to tell them apart when the names are covered.

One triple a run, only at the start of its first bubble (before: one a bubble). Why: a triple spends three of the ten words rule 62 allows, and a triple in every bubble turns her into a tic instead of a voice.

Struck 'arre' from her mouth entirely: the comfort triple 'Arre, arre, arre.' becomes 'Aao, aao, aao. Idhar baitho.', and 'arre' leaves her uses list. Why: C6 and table 2.15, 'arre' lives only in Captain sahab's 'Arre waah'.

Struck 'Ek-ek karke' from her order sample and uses ('Chalo, chalo, chalo! Bade wale upar! Jaldi!' instead). Why: it is your once-a-year cross line (2.11), and 'ek' is a number word in a voice that has none.
Sorry loses 'Lo,': 'Sorry, sorry, sorry! Lo, pehle khao.' becomes 'Sorry, sorry, sorry! Pehle khao.' Why: 'Lo.' is Mausa ji's alone (C6, C8, table 2.15).
'Pehle khao, phir baat.' becomes 'Na, na, na! Khaali pet baat nahin!', and 'Pehle khao' is the only 'Pehle' she keeps. Why: C9, the 'first X, then Y' courtesy is yours.

Thanks is now a spoken line of her own, a teacher's grade: 'Ekdum first class!' (before: 'in words, with food', never fixed). Added how she takes thanks: 'Haaye! Zor se kaho! Amma bhi sunein!'. Why: table 2.14 gives each person one way to thank, and her want (to be the one Amma thanks) and fear (that nobody hears her) belong in that line; December's silence stays the one time thanks quiets her.
Her joke's 'Teesri class' becomes 'Meri class'. Why: ordinals leave everyone's speech (2.15), and her numbers stay at none.

Dropped the English verb + kar/ho frame ('adjust karo', 'share karo') and never 'late ho gaye'. Why: 2.2 makes that frame Mummy's alone; her English now carries only feeling and school words (sorry, tension, first class, topper, homework, copy, teacher, fail, late mark), which no one else's English carries (2.12 mix row).

Her words now come from her teaching as well as her kitchen: 'Late mark!', 'Aaj teacher fail!', 'meri class ka inaam', 'Copiyan upar!', the riddle-setter's 'bujhiye'. Why: the comics review's type test found her teaching invisible in her only chapter, which leaves the stock loud aunt who feeds; this puts the teacher in her mouth without the chapter 1 note words (maths, coaching, teaches).

Her question-she-answers-herself is now tied to her riddles ('Kiski? Hamari!'), and 'Kisne karwaayi?' at the lower berth is marked as the one question she cannot answer herself. Why: it gives the tic a reason in who she is, and makes the moved silence land.

Added a guard to her exclamation: 'Haaye' never doubled or tripled. Why: हाय-हाय is a lament and a protest chant, and her triple habit would otherwise reach for it; the existing guard (never followed by a name of god or 'Maa') stays.

Love key kept and owned: 'Haaye! Bahut yaad aayi.' is hers alone, and a parting form in the same key added: 'Abhi se yaad aa rahi!'. Why: C16, Mama ji gives up 'Bahut' for 'Roz.'; hers is loud and to the room with food, his warm and one to one with a hug.
The shout (1.09) and the temper line now answer themselves ('Kabhi nahin!', 'Nahin!'), so even her biggest lines carry her shape. Neither is the ask (rule 37) and neither reacts to a pick (rule 39).

New lines between her and others: Amma, Chhoti, Papa, Munna, Aji, Bhabhi, Tinku and Masterji. Why: C15, almost no line in the cast passed between people other than you, so the voice test never heard her with them.

Typing: the voice-note close 'aur haan, khana kha lena' becomes 'chalo, khana kha lena' (Mama ji's joiner); the voice-note card shows no length figure and the 4:10 am note no longer opens 'ek baat, ek baat, ek baat'; no typed figures of any kind; 🙏 is out until the owner decides; two new samples (your good news, her typed hurt). Why: her numbers are none on screen too, and her typed signs must not borrow another file's.

Words to her are unchanged: every address word (Amma, Chhoti, no word for Papa, Munna, Aji, Bhabhi, the titles) and every word for her stays as the file has it, all waiting on the readers' address table (rule 65).

Open points for readers and the test: whether 'Meri class bhi girati hai' and 'Late mark' sound right to a Hindi-first reader; and if the English blind sort mixes her 'Oh!' up with Mama ji's 'Oho!', keep 'Haaye!' in English mode, as Mami keeps 'Ish'.

Kept: her essence, want, fear, contradiction, year arc, the shout's place, the lower-berth silence, the December silence, every never-rule on harassment and dowry reports, and the note-word limits. Only how she speaks changed.

voices.name: Mausa ji (मौसा जी), about 58, chapter 2's voice

voice.register: Bare, low and flat: the slowest voice in the cast, with long silences that his hands fill. One to five counted words a bubble (names and kin words not counted, as in rule 62; his own cap, well inside rule 62's ten), usually two short pieces: an opener ('Hmm.', 'Hain?', 'Lo.' or the thing itself), then the state of a thing. His sentence has no person in it. The subject is a thing (the wire, the bench, the board, the food, the job) and it gets a verdict or a state: 'Taar dheela.', 'Bench theek hai.', 'Khana thanda.' Verbs survive only in plain logistics, with the pronoun dropped ('Aata hoon.', 'Garam karta hoon.', 'Ho gaya.'). His only orders are to rest ('So jao.') and to keep hands off live current ('Switch mat chhoona.'). He answers rather than asks; his few questions are about sleep, water or a drip. Every bubble is followed, in the same panel or the next, by something his hands do. When a beat needs more, he speaks again only after a deed, so a run is two bubbles with an action between them, never two bubbles back to back. He talks most to whoever should be resting (you, at the ward). Told apart from the other short voices: Nani gives people verbless orders and grocer's proverbs; Captain sahab calls in English cricket words, the call then the reason; Tinku gives a score and 'haan?'; you name the listener. He names almost nobody, counts nothing and never says 'I'.
voice.mix: Bare Hindi, the plainest in the cast. No proverb or idiom (Nani's), no Urdu shop courtesy such as 'Dekhiye', fikr or farq (Masterji's), no English feeling words such as tension, sorry or relax (Mausi's), no English verb with kar or ho (Mummy's), no whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's). English comes in only as his trade's nouns, used as Hindi nouns (current, line, fuse, meter, earthing, board, switch, wiring, joint), and the hospital words everyone uses (BP, drip, ward, X-ray). Where everyday Hindi has its own word he takes it: 'bijli' for power, 'taar' for wire. Never 'main switch' or 'mains' in Hinglish, because 'main' reads as मैं. Hinglish mode is Roman Hindi with those nouns. English mode stays as short as the Hindi, puts the thing first and leaves himself out ('Food's cold. Warming it.', 'Lights on, then.'), and keeps one English word for each verdict, so the English sort still hears him: mazboot is 'solid', dheela is 'loose', theek is 'fine'.
tics: The thing, then its verdict or its state: 'Taar dheela.' | 'Board theek.' | 'Khana thanda.' The subject is never a person, himself included.

'Hmm.' | 'हम्म।' before an answer, or as the whole answer, in at most one bubble in three and never two bubbles running; otherwise one slow nod. In chapter 2's three or four bubbles that is once. When he is moved, the 'Hmm' becomes a cleared throat and a look at the window.
No 'I': first-person verbs only for plain logistics, with the pronoun dropped ('Abhi aaya.', 'Aata hoon.', 'Dekh liya.').

One-word verdicts, now his alone: 'Theek.' | 'ठीक।' (fine), 'Mazboot.' | 'मज़बूत।' (solid: a good joint, good work, Amma ji; his highest word), 'Dheela.' | 'ढीला।' (loose, sloppy: of a joint, a wire or a job, never of cloth, which is Masterji's word, and never of a person).
