OPEN FOR THE BLIND SORT: Masterji's target also says 'dheela' (of cloth). Mausa ji's 'dheela' is only ever said of a joint, a wire or a job. If readers mix the two up on it three times or more, his fallback is 'kachcha' ('Joint kachcha.' | 'जोड़ कच्चा।' | 'Weak joint.'), said of work only.

FOR THE READERS: 'Hain?' in Hinglish; 'जोड़' or 'जॉइंट' in Hindi mode; 'Amma ji's solid.' in English; whether the missed call still reads true; and the rule 66 flags listed under address, each cleared by a native reader.

voices.name: Masterji (मास्टरजी), about 60, the tailor next door; chapter 3's voice

voice.register: Slow, warm and unhurried: the station road's slow measurer, the slowest of the cast's four long runners (Papa speaks in exact whole sentences, Mausi fast and tripled, Mama ji in one run-on). SHAPE (his alone): a verdict first, short and sure, then a wander to cloth or weather, hinged on 'Waise' ('Mind you'). A run is two or three bubbles, budgeted as pairs so the wander is never the line that gets cut; each bubble is one or two short sentences of 4 to 10 words, and in a single bubble the verdict and the turn both show. Full stops throughout, even after 'Uff.'; no exclamation marks; he asks a question only when he wants the answer, and never answers his own the way Mausi does (the fixed ending's 'Whose drain? Let the lane cup decide.' hands the question on to the cup). NUMBERS: none in speech. Time is only 'bas abhi' (right away, which means an hour), and he blames the trains; the past is dated by what was on his machine ('the year of Bhai sahab's jacket'), never a year or a count of years (rule 2). A measure by feel ('ungli bhar', 'baal bhar', 'baalisht') comes at most once in a run, so it never becomes a counting tic. His exactness shows in plain verdicts: straight, crooked, level, loose, tight (of cloth, never of a person). FEELING: said out loud but sideways, in pictures of cloth and weather ('Wet cloth dries. It's the torn cloth you worry about.'); never the plain feeling words Mausi and Mama ji own, and never only a deed. HUMOUR: kind and whimsical. He gives the weather, the mud, the drain, clocks and cloth moods of their own: the sky sulks, the mud sleeps late, the drain is stubborn, clocks swell in the monsoon. The joke is at the road, the sky or himself, never at a person's body or a woman's clothes, and he is never its butt. WHEN CROSS (at things only: the drain, the sky, cheap cloth): the wander stops. One short verdict, silence, and he straightens out of his stoop. He never raises his voice; Mummy, his chapter's other voice, gets more polite instead, so their tells never match. TALKS MOST TO whoever stands still long enough (you, most of all), and to Captain sahab across the drain.
voice.mix: Soft bazaar Hindustani: a Hindi frame carrying the everyday Urdu-rooted words of an old market that every community in the Hindi belt uses (fikr, farq, mausam, mizaaj, waqt, zaroor, khair, waise, afwaah, astar), with tailoring English used only as Hindi nouns (fitting, trial, size, finish, pattern, shutter, and 'ready-made', said with a sniff). His tailoring verbs are Hindi: naapna, kaatna, silna, kholna (let out), kasna (take in); never an English verb with kar or ho, which is Mummy's frame, and never a whole English clause, which is Mama ji's and Mami's. No markedly Urdu courtesy forms (janaab, aadaab, farmaiye, huzoor, tashreef, khuda hafiz), so the register reads as an old bazaar and not as a community; a Hindi-first and an Urdu-speaking reader confirm (rule 65). In Hinglish mode his lines are Roman Hindi with those nouns. In English mode the habits carry over as unhurried, slightly old-fashioned courtesy: 'Look,' for 'Dekhiye', 'Mind you,' for 'Waise', 'Ugh.' for 'Uff.', 'level', 'a finger out', 'right away', and the cloth and weather pictures intact. No accent is ever spelled out (the funny-shopkeeper trap in the realism notes).
tics: Verdict first, then 'Waise' and a wander to cloth or weather. 'Waise' / 'Mind you' as a hinge is his alone in the cast (proposed for the one-owner table, matrix 2.15).
Opens with 'Dekhiye' / 'Look,' to everyone, Tinku and you included: a counter habit, not a respect form. At most one line in three, so it stays a habit and not a stamp. 'Dekho' is not his.
Gives weather, mud, the drain, clocks and cloth moods: 'Aasmaan rootha hai', 'Keechad abhi so raha hai', 'Naali ziddi hai', 'Mausam ka mizaaj bigda hai'. This whimsy is his humour.
Reads the weather from the feel of cloth (limp means rain, stiff or crisp means sun) and is right; the chapter uses his forecasts.
Dates the past by what was on his machine ('Bhai sahab ki jacket wala saal', 'Mama ji ki interview wali kameez'); never a year, never a count of years.
Gives every time as 'bas abhi', which means an hour, and blames the trains when he is late; never a clock time.
A measure by feel at most once in a run: 'ungli bhar' (a finger's width), 'baal bhar' (a hair's breadth), 'baalisht' (a hand span). Never a figure, because his tape lost its marks.

Tailoring pictures for whatever he cannot say straight: a road needs stitching, a person is an old garment relined, a family's stitching stays home when the cloth travels. Never a picture of anyone's body.
Holds his right thumb and forefinger a finger's width apart while he talks.
'Uff.' with a full stop is his only exclamation, at things, never at a person.
When cross, the wander stops: one short verdict, silence, and he straightens out of the stoop.
catchphrases: 'Bas abhi.' | 'बस अभी।' | 'Right away.' His only way of giving a time; it means an hour. (No figure.)
'Barabar.' | 'बराबर।' | 'Level.' His one-word praise, then a tug of the tape ends. In Hindi it also means 'equal', a quiet echo in a fairness game that nobody ever points out.
'Kapde ka bhi mizaaj hota hai.' | 'कपड़े का भी मिज़ाज होता है।' | 'Cloth has its moods too.' His answer to a forecast, a bad cut or a bad week: his own saying, not a proverb (proverbs are Nani's).
voice.exclamation: 'Uff.' | 'उफ़्फ़।' | English mode 'Ugh.' A sound with no religious meaning, for exasperation at things: the drain, the sky, cheap cloth, a power cut. Always a full stop, never an exclamation mark; nobody else in the cast uses it, and it fills the place where an elder would reach for a god-word (rule 3). For joy he has no cry: he says 'Achha?' and claims the good news was in the cloth all along.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: he re-measures, out loud, and lets the cloth forgive: 'Chalo, phir se naap lete hain. Waise kapda bura nahin maanta.' | 'चलो, फिर से नाप लेते हैं। वैसे कपड़ा बुरा नहीं मानता।' | 'Come, we measure again. Mind you, cloth never minds.' He never says 'sorry' (Mausi's), 'maaf kijiye' (yours) or 'galti hui' (Mausa ji's), and never 'I'm late' (the trains were). THANKS: he names the season after the favour, the way he dates his past by garments: 'Ab ye tumhari chai wali barsaat.' | 'अब ये तुम्हारी चाय वाली बरसात।' | 'This is the monsoon of your tea now.' To an elder: 'Ab ye barsaat aapke naam.' When he is thanked, he makes the favour small and names the season anyway ('Kinari hi toh thi.'). Never 'shukriya' (yours), 'thank you' (Mami's, to strangers), 'paise nahin loonga' or any 'no charge' (Mummy owns 'Iska bill nahin.'). LOVE: his time. The tumbler set down beside you and a story offered, said out loud: 'Chai yahin. Abhi garam hai.' then 'Waise, Bhai sahab ki jacket wali baat sunaaoon?' At a parting it is said sideways in cloth: 'Kapda door jaaye, silai yahin ki rehti hai.' | 'Cloth travels far. The stitching stays here.' Never 'yaad aayi', 'I missed you' or 'love' (Mausi's and Mama ji's plain words).

JUDGING NOTES (chapter 3's cards only, with his face chip; unchanged by this pass): his idiom is how people are as customers (fidgets through every fitting, never collects the stitching, has every seam redone, wants everything by tomorrow), landing on women and men equally; punctuality stays off his notes (rule 20).
never: Any figure in speech: no inches, minutes, hours, prices, scores, ordinals, years or counts of years (rule 2); no 'sharp', no 'about', 'roughly' or लगभग for a measure. The number leaners are Papa and Tinku.
A measure by feel in every verdict: once a run at most.
'Pehle' in any shape ('Pehle chai' is struck: 'Pehle ___' is yours).
'Paise nahin loonga', 'no charge' or any bill-free thanks (Mummy's 'Iska bill nahin.').
'Sorry' (Mausi's), 'maaf kijiye' and 'shukriya' (yours), 'thank you' (Mami's, to strangers), 'galti hui' (Mausa ji's), 'galat nikla' (Papa's).

Another person's word or shape: 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' as one-word lines (Mausa ji), 'arre' (Captain sahab), 'pakka' (struck), 'Dekho' (not his), 'Suno' and 'hai na?' (Mausi), 'haan?' (Tinku), 'Correct?' (Mami), 'aur haan' (Mama ji), 'Kamaal' (Papa), 'bahut yaad' and 'I missed you' (Mausi, Mama ji), 'not out' or any cricket call (Captain sahab, Tinku).
An English verb with kar or ho ('alter karna', 'check karo'), or a whole English clause.
A proverb: proverbs are Nani's register; his sayings are his own pictures.
Hurrying anyone, 'jaldi' about his own work, or 'I'm late'.
Any word on a woman's dress, its length, tightness or modesty (no छोटा or तंग of clothes on a woman, no शर्म, इज़्ज़त, 'decent', 'modern'), or on anyone's body size (no मोटा, पतला).
'Bossy', 'argues', रौब, बहस, or any note about women or men in general.
'Ready-made' as praise.

Markedly Urdu courtesy forms (janaab, aadaab, farmaiye, huzoor, tashreef, khuda hafiz) and any religious word: no god's name, blessing, festival word, 'shukr hai', 'tauba', 'Khuda', 'Rab', 'Bhagwan'; in English mode no 'Goodness', 'Heavens', 'Good grief', 'Lord', 'Oh my' (rule 3).
Beta, beti, bhaiya, didi or any gendered word for you; any future or helper-verb past that changes with your gender in a line to you (rule 66).
A card person's name, or any word from a note on that decision's cards, in a bubble (rule 36).
Any doubt of a report of harassment or bullying, or of a dowry demand, or calling one a misunderstanding (rule 22).
An exclamation mark, a raised voice, or temper at a person.
address: Nani: 'Nani ji', आप ('Ab dhoondhiye'). She calls him 'Master'.
Mummy: 'Bhabhi ji', आप. She calls him 'Masterji', आप.
Papa: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Papa says 'Masterji', आप.
Mama ji: 'Mama ji', आप, now that he is a grown customer. Mama ji says 'Masterji', आप.
Tinku: 'Tinku', तुम. She says 'Masterji', आप.
Mausi: 'Mausi ji', आप. Mausa ji: 'Mausa ji', आप both ways. Mami: 'Mami ji', आप.
Captain sahab: 'Captain' (कप्तान), dropping the sahab, with आप; thirty monsoons of familiarity, not rudeness. Captain sahab calls him 'Master', आप.
Customers and strangers: 'Dekhiye' and आप, every time.

YOU (rule 66): no address word at all. तुम only in commands ('वो ईंट लाओ। सिरे पर रख दो।'), 'who should' asks ('थान छत पर कौन ले जाए?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('अब ये तुम्हारी चाय वाली बरसात।', where तुम्हारी agrees with चाय). 'Dekhiye' reaches you too, as his counter habit. Once in the year, teasing, आप: 'अब तो आप इंचार्ज हैं।' Never बेटा, भैया, दीदी; never आओगे/आओगी, थके हो, आ गए; any flagged line (such as one ending in a verb that agrees with the mud or the stitching) goes to the native reader.
From you to him: 'Masterji' and आप with -इए ('बैठिए, मास्टरजी।'); your one fixed reply 'Bas abhi, Masterji.' is verbless and gender-free.
This list follows the cast map's one address table where it differs; the Hindi-first and South Indian readers sign it off (rule 65).
samples: VERDICT AND WANDER (3.02, his flooded doorway, to Mummy at her half-raised shutter; the first line as drafted, the wander now hinged on 'Waise'): EN 'All this mud, by Saturday?' / 'Mind you, the sky's still sulking.' | HINGLISH 'Itna keechad, Shanivaar tak?' / 'Waise aasmaan abhi bhi rootha hai.' | HINDI 'इतना कीचड़, शनिवार तक?' / 'वैसे आसमान अभी भी रूठा है।'

A VERDICT ON A HEM (to a customer at a fitting; his one measure by feel in this run): EN 'Look, the edge is a finger out.' / 'Mind you, the cloth's gone limp today. Rain's coming.' | HINGLISH 'Dekhiye, kinari ungli bhar tedhi.' / 'Waise kapda bhi aaj dheela hai. Barsaat aayegi.' | HINDI 'देखिए, किनारी उँगली भर टेढ़ी।' / 'वैसे कपड़ा भी आज ढीला है। बरसात आएगी।'

TEASE (to Mummy, her shutter up at nine and his still down): EN 'Up already, Bhabhi ji?' / 'Even the mud's still asleep.' | HINGLISH 'Itni jaldi, Bhabhi ji?' / 'Keechad bhi abhi so raha hai.' | HINDI 'इतनी जल्दी, भाभी जी?' / 'कीचड़ भी अभी सो रहा है।'

voices.name: Captain sahab (कप्तान साहब), about 65

voice.register: Crisp and low: an umpire's carrying voice that never needs raising. HIS SHAPE IS THE CALL. Every line opens on an umpire's call or a coach's word, then at most one short reason or instruction, 2 to 7 words in one bubble, with a pause after the call as if the ball were still in the air ('No ball. A rule's a rule.', 'Wait. Clouds over the depot end.'). The calls do the work of yes and no: 'Not out.' (yes, fine, carry on), 'Out.' (no, finished), 'No ball.' (not allowed, does not count), 'Wait.' (not yet), 'Over.' (done, enough), 'Dead ball.' (take that back), 'Last over.' (nearly time). He stretches the umpire's list over everyday life: a late guest is 'Timed out.', his knee is 'Retired hurt.', a rumour is an appeal he turns down. Short, but not like the cast's other short voices: Nani closes bare fragments with no call, Mausa ji drops the subject, Tinku gives a score and 'haan?', you name the listener. Beside Tinku in chapter 4 he gives verdicts and she keeps the score: he never describes play as it happens (her commentary) and never says a score. FEELING is coded in a call: 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji.' means you are all right; 'Front foot.' is love for every child he coached; 'Well played.' comes once a year, and then he looks away. HUMOUR: sardonic and bone-dry, about his knee, his age and the game, never about a person's hard fact; while rulebook Q5 is open his jokes stay out of the chapter outcome (rule 46). NUMBERS: rare and marked, only the toss countdown in the two lead-ins (a story deadline, rule 37) and 'Nine means nine' once a year to Papa; everything else in words, so lateness is 'Timed out', never two hours. CROSS: he goes still. A whisper bubble, the calls further apart, the verdict finger up and kept up; never a shout, never an exclamation mark. Tinku, his chapter's other voice, goes fast when cross, so their tells never match. TALKS MOST TO the lane's players, and on the page to Tinku at the scorer's table, Papa on the six o'clock walk and Masterji across the drain. He is never the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame, with English only as whole cricket calls and coaching words (out, not out, no ball, dead ball, over, last over, timed out, retired hurt, next ball, front foot, straight bat, well played, well fielded, well left, clean catch, crease, toss, pitch) and a few bus-depot nouns (servicing, jack, clutch, tube, tarpaulin, depot). That is the older speakers' pattern in the realism notes, with the topic pulling the English in ('Captain sahab talks cricket in English nouns'). He never switches a whole clause into English (Mama ji and Mami do) and never uses an English verb with kar or ho (Mummy's frame alone), which is why his knee is 'Retired hurt', a call, and never 'retire hua'. The calls are the same words in all three modes, so his Hinglish and his Hindi read almost the same: in Devanagari the calls stay English (नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, डेड बॉल, नेक्स्ट बॉल, वेल फ़ील्डेड, टाइम्ड आउट), as people on a lane say them. The one call that changes is 'Wait': 'Ruko' | 'रुको' to anyone he has coached, 'Rukiye' | 'रुकिए' to an elder. Around the calls, plain lane Hindi: आप and a title to elders, तुम to anyone he has coached or seen drop a catch. English mode: plain, clipped English with the calls unchanged.

Answers yes and no with a call, in all three modes: 'Not out.' (yes), 'Out.' (no), 'Wait.' (not yet), 'Over.' (enough). His typed yes is 'Not out' too.

habits: The phone: a plain phone in a plain dark case with a cracked top corner, kept in a trouser pocket. Painted with a blank screen; every message is live text on it, or a message card under the panel if the phone is small (rules 30 and 40). No app name, app look or 'forwarded' label (rule 3), and no quirk about his eyes or the font size.

Script: English in Latin letters only, never Devanagari and never a Hinglish sentence (realism notes 2.3). The messages are strings of nouns and calls, not English clauses, so this does not break his speech's no-clause rule.
Shape (changed): a telegram in his speaking shape, the call or the thing first, then the place, then one instruction, 1 to 7 words. It no longer opens on a time.
His typed yes is 'Not out', his not-yet 'Wait', his enough 'Over'. He never types 'ok' (Tinku's 'k', Mausa ji's 'Ok.', Masterji's 'ok ji') or 'Noted' (Papa's).
Figures: none, except the cup's date and its nine o'clock, as digits and only in cup messages. Never a minute (Papa's), never a score (Tinku's), never a price.

Punctuation: none at all, not even a question mark. The phone capitalises the first letter, and that is his only capital. Never all capitals, which reads as shouting and is the 'WhatsApp uncle' trap (realism notes 7).
The one exception: once a year, in his own family group (mentioned, never shown), he writes the cup's end in full sentences with full stops. That is the tell that it matters.
Emoji: one only, 🏏, on cup messages. Tinku's 🏏 to him copies his. No faces, no folded hands, no stickers, no good-morning flowers (Papa's), no forwards, ever.
Voice notes: never sends one. He listens to the first few seconds of anyone else's and answers with the one fact asked, or a call.

He sends the same words one by one to every person rather than to a group: he trusts a message he has sent himself. The lane's group exists and is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct: no group chat).
Reads and answers twice a day, after the walk and before the toss, and within a minute about cricket or the drain; never late at night (he walks at dawn).
One forefinger, slow and deliberate; no typos, because there are so few words.

changed: KEPT: who he is. Essence, want, fear, contradiction (strict by the book, still sore about one trial), the turn at 4.26 ('That book. Show the district.'), the stakes line at 4.03, the fixed ending at 4.27, 'Straight bat. Front foot.', 'My one trial. Not out. Ask anyone.', the toss as his word alone, and the still, whispering anger.

SHAPE (C2): the call stays his sentence shape, but the list of calls grows (Dead ball, Last over, Timed out, Retired hurt), so the calls carry everyday meaning off the ground and his voice is a grammar, not a pile of cricket nouns. Why: the reviews asked each clipped speaker for a shape of their own, not only trade words.

NUMBERS (C1): 'your best score', said when you come home, leaves his speech; he names your shot instead ('Front foot. Cross bat, abhi bhi?'). 'Nine means nine' moves from his catchphrases to one marked line a year to Papa; the toss countdown stays only in the two lead-ins (rule 37). Lateness becomes 'Timed out', never a figure. Why: only Papa and Tinku lean on numbers.

SORRY (C4): 'Next ball.' alone was a swap, moving on without owning anything. Now: 'Dead ball. Umpire ki chook. Next ball.', which takes the call back, owns it, then moves on. 'Next ball' stays inside it, so the target card still matches. Why: the reviews named him among the seven elders who never said sorry.

THANKS (C4): 'Well fielded.' is now said out loud, with the person's title, beside the old deeds (the full price on Mummy's counter: 'Well fielded, Bhabhi ji.'). When he is thanked: 'Over.' and the credit sent elsewhere. Why: thanks had been only a deed.

COMFORT (C7): 'Not out, Bhabhi ji. Next ball.' becomes 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.' A bare 'Not out.' stays his verdict, never comfort. Why: he and Tinku both said 'Not out' to Mummy at one beat (Tinku's line is now 'Match tie').
LOVE (C3): 'Front foot.' stays, and now reaches you on the platform and at the door in words ('Front foot. Seedha bat, wahan bhi.'), not as a number kept in silence.
THE KNEE JOKE: 'Ghutna retire hua. Main nahin.' becomes 'Retired hurt. Sirf ghutna.' Why: 'retire hua' is an English verb with ho, Mummy's frame alone; 'Retired hurt' is a call.
HIS FEAR: 'Maidan chhota ho raha hai, Bhai sahab.' becomes 'Last over, Bhai sahab. Maidan pe scooter.' Why: call first; the fear stays coded in a call.
MAMA JI'S TEASE: 'Catch bhi, trophy bhi. Dono chhoote.' becomes 'Catch? Trophy bhi chhooti.' Why: call first; the doubled 'X bhi, Y bhi' read like a list (Mummy's shape).

ONE FORM IN EVERY MODE: Hinglish 'Agli gend.' and Hindi 'अगली गेंद।' become 'Next ball.' and 'नेक्स्ट बॉल।'. Why: his marker is that his Hinglish and Hindi read alike, and the catch-line should sort in all three modes.

WORDS HANDED TO THEIR OWNERS (C6, C9, matrix 2.15): 'chalo' and 'dekho' leave his commands to you (Mausi's and Masterji's); 'full service' becomes 'servicing' (bare 'full' is Mama ji's); 'Bad light stops play' and every score or commentary shape stay Tinku's; 'arre' lives only in his 'Arre waah', never sarcastic, never followed by a name.

HEARD WITH THE OTHERS (C15): samples and test lines now go to Mausa ji (the lights), Mama ji (late), Masterji (the tea, the drain), Papa (the clock, the walk), Tinku (the shade, the no-ball), Mummy (the rumour, the flood), Nani (the trial) and a child, not mostly to you.
C10 DODGE: asked how he is, he no longer answers with a number; 'Not out. Ghutna servicing mein.' is a real answer, his knee, in a call.

TYPING: the telegram now opens on the call or the thing, not on a time. Figures only the cup's date and its nine, in cup messages. '6' to Papa becomes 'Route clear' (clocks are Papa's); 'Scorer 8 30 table 2 pencils' becomes 'Scorer chair in shade bring book'; 'bring water' goes ('water' is a chapter 4 note word); 'Catch first' becomes 'Catch' (an English 'first' sat on your 'Pehle ___'); 'Cup done.' becomes 'The cup is over.' ('done' is Mami's status word); his typed yes is 'Not out'.

KNOCK-ON FOR HIS CAST FILE AND OTHERS: his YOU relationship ('your best score ... the only number about you he keeps' becomes 'your shot'), his MUMMY relationship ('Not out, Bhabhi ji. Next ball.' becomes the new comfort line), his PAPA relationship and Papa's file ('6' becomes 'Route clear'), and the cast map's sound grid row ('commentary cadence' becomes 'umpire's calls', since commentary is Tinku's; its sample 'bring water' goes) and realism notes 2.3 ('9 am sharp' uses Papa's 'sharp').

FOR THE READERS (rule 65): Hindi-first readers check 'Dead ball' as a sorry (fallback 'Call wapas. Next ball.'), 'Timed out' (fallback 'Out. Late matlab out.'), 'Retired hurt', 'अंपायर की चूक', 'खिलाड़ी' for any child, and 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin' (उँगली उठाना also means to accuse, which is the point).

voices.name: Mami (मामी), about 45

voice.register: Medium and even, in two parts. Her lead shape is the readback: 'So.' | 'तो।' | 'Toh.', then one whole sentence that hands your own plan back to you, then 'Correct?' | 'सही?' | 'Sahi?', and she waits for the answer. Her second shape is the status pair: a thing, a comma, its status, a full stop, then the next pair ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.'). The item is named, never numbered: no ordinals, no counts, no prices, no clock times. A bubble runs 4 to 10 words, most often 6 to 9; usually one bubble, at most two (the readback, then a status). Crisp, unhurried and never raised: no exclamation mark in any bubble, 'Ish.' included, and never the shout (the chapter's shout is Mama ji's). The same pace in a crisis as at tea, which is why people calm down near her. She answers a question with a status, never a feeling, and files her own feelings the same way ('Status: guest.'). Firm with vendors, polite with elders, sly with her husband. Talked over, she raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes her pair when the room is quiet. When cross she goes slower, turns the clipboard round to face the person, reads the line aloud from it ('It's written here.') and closes with an icy 'Thank you' to a vendor, or a flat 'Correct?' to family. Apart from the cast: not Mummy's comma lists of jobs and people with no status ('Aur kuch?'), not Mausa ji's verbless verdicts on things (no English, no comma pairs), not Captain sahab's call then reason, not Papa's whole sentences with a time in them, not Nani's jobs handed to 'koi'. A script can count it: about two lines in three carry a status word or end on 'Correct?'; none carries an ordinal or a figure; none carries '!'.
voice.mix: City whole-clause switching, the younger urban pattern in the realism notes (the Dehradun code-switching study): she switches at the full stop, a whole Hindi clause and then a whole English one, or the other way round ('Meri shaadi ki bhi list thi. Still on file.'). Inside a Hindi clause only the desk's nouns cross over (list, item, form, file, claim, receipt, balance). Her English carries statuses and the desk: done, pending, not known, safe, approved, in progress, closed, open, on file, nothing outstanding, not on the list, correct, thank you. Her Hindi carries people, food, rooms and elders. In Hinglish bubbles the status stays English ('Chaabiyan, pending.'); in Hindi mode it becomes the everyday Hindi a city office speaks (हो गया, पेंडिंग, पता नहीं, बाक़ी, मंज़ूर, चालू, बंद, खुली, फ़ाइल में, सलामत), and 'Thank you' stays English (थैंक यू) in every mode, because it is the counter's word. Polite Hindi to every elder and every vendor (आप, -इए). One Bengali word, her mother's: the exclamation 'Ish.' Nothing else from Bengali, and never a spelled accent. Apart from Mama ji, who leads with fast English and runs his clauses together on 'aur haan', she is clause by clause, each one closed, and her English is the desk's, never logistics talk, slang or 'Don't worry'. Apart from Mummy, she never builds an English verb with kar or ho ('check karo' is Mummy's); her English verbs stay inside English clauses.
tics: THE READBACK, her lead tic: 'So.', your plan in one whole sentence, 'Correct?', and she waits: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ तुम्हारे पास, आज रात से। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?'. From Friday she stops reading your plan back to you, and that is the nearest she comes to thanking you.
THE STATUS PAIR: thing, comma, status, full stop: 'Tent, done. Cook, pending. Keys, not known.' It replaces the ordinals: she names the item, never its place on the list.
She files herself the same way. Asked how she is: 'Me? Nothing outstanding.' | 'मैं? कुछ बाक़ी नहीं।' | 'Main? Koi balance nahin.' Hurt, said once and dry: 'Status: guest.'

Asks every vendor and helper about their children, the counter's habit and her one interest on the page that is not a list: 'Bhaiya ji, beti ka paper kaisa gaya?'. It is also, quietly, about her own daughter.
'Thank you' out loud, in English, to every vendor and stranger, even when cross, and never to family (Mausi teases her for saying it 'like a bill').
'Tick.' | 'टिक।' as praise and thanks to family, and the pen comes down as she says it.
Sly about her husband, said as a status and to the young ones, as if he were not standing there: 'Your Mama ji: still pending.'
Wants paper behind any claim: a rumour or a promise gets 'Status, not known.' and 'Is it in writing?'
Talked over: raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes her pair when the room is quiet. (The draft's 'Ek minute' stays gone: it was your temper line.)
Never a rhetorical or a stacked question (those are Mausi's); every question she asks has one answer, and she waits for it.
Days of the week, never a clock time and never 'soon': 'by Saturday', 'Thursday evening'.
No exclamation mark anywhere, spoken or typed, not even for 'Ish.'

THE STATUS PAIR: 'Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.' | 'चाबियाँ, पेंडिंग। लिफ़ाफ़े, हो गए।' | 'Chaabiyan, pending. Lifafe, done.' (writers keep it away from any decision whose cards use keys or envelopes, rule 36)

HER NO: 'Not on the list.' | 'लिस्ट में नहीं है।' | 'List mein nahin hai.' Turned round once, at the first slice: 'Ish. That wasn't on my list.' | 'इश्श। ये मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं था।' | 'Ish. Ye meri list mein nahin tha.' (None of the three carries a number.)
voice.exclamation: 'Ish.' | 'इश्श।' | 'Ish.' (kept as 'Ish.' in English mode too, as her own sound). New. Her mother's Bengali word for dismay, sympathy and embarrassed surprise ('oh no', 'oh dear'); in her it also covers the rare happy surprise that catches her out (the good news, the first slice). Said flat and low, closed with a full stop, never with '!', never with a giggle or a hand to the mouth. No religious meaning. At most once a scene. Nobody else in the cast uses it; it strikes her old 'Lo.', which is Mausa ji's. Two reader checks: a Bengali reader confirms the sense; a Hindi-first reader confirms it is not heard as ईश ('lord', the root of Ishwar, banned by rule 3; ईश has a long ई and one श, इश्श a short इ and a doubled श) or as the coy 'इश्श' of old Hindi films, which would turn the calmest woman in the cast into a blushing type. If either reader hears it so, the fallback is 'Ajeeb.' | 'अजीब।' | 'Odd.', which nobody else uses either.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, the same to family, vendors and you: the fault filed as her own item, 'Mera item tha. Chhoot gaya.' | 'मेरा आइटम था। छूट गया।' | 'That was my item. It slipped.', and the right entry at once, aloud ('Didi, write Saturday.'). Never the English 'sorry' (Mausi's alone). THANKS, GIVEN: to family, 'Tick.' | 'टिक।' | 'Tick.' as the pen comes down; to vendors and strangers, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.', English in every mode; to you, from Friday, she stops reading your plan back, and her typed lists to you lose their 'Correct?' line. THANKS, RECEIVED: 'Thank you counter ke liye hai. Yahan bas tick.' | 'थैंक यू काउंटर के लिए है। यहाँ बस टिक।' | 'Thank-yous are for the counter. Here, just a tick.' LOVE: never in plain words; filed, and left open. It is the one line she never ticks, 'Beti ka bag', at the top of every wedding list, and the pen held over it on the wedding evening; Mama ji's item, which she always ticks first, and his hand, the only one allowed to write on her list; and, at a parting, the one status she will not close: 'Your file: open. Always.' | 'तुम्हारी फ़ाइल: खुली। हमेशा।' | 'Tumhari file: open. Hamesha.'

habits: DEVICE: a large-screen smartphone in a plain navy-blue case, text at the normal size, kept in her bag and out only for a call (at her right ear, the pen slid into the clipboard's clip) or for the night's list. Two quick thumbs. A plain power bank for everyone else's phones. In chapter 5 her phone stays off screen, like Mama ji's.

SCRIPT: Roman letters only, in the city's Hinglish: English items and statuses, Hindi people and verbs ('Rooms done. Chaabiyan kiske paas?'). Never Devanagari, which is too slow for her. Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages; her lines to you mark no gender ('You take over Thu evening').

FORMAT: one item per line, a capitalised noun and its status symbol, with a comma before any detail ('Keys, yours ✅'). No line numbers and no digits in any message on screen: that is the typing half of the number cap. No full stops at line ends, no whole words in capitals (capitals read as shouting, realism), no exclamation mark. The first line names the list and the day ('Wedding list, Thu'). On every wedding list the second line is 'Beti ka bag', with no symbol, the only line she never gives a status; then 'Papa, trains ✅', the one item she never has to chase. Family lists end on 'Correct?'; vendor lists end on 'Thank you'.

APART FROM THE OTHERS: Papa types single facts with full stops and times, Mummy lowercase one-liners that end on a figure, Tinku lowercase stretched letters and scores, and you the lowercase colon form ('keys: sorted'), which is why her detail takes a comma, not a colon.
STATUS SYMBOLS, her only emoji: ✅ done, ⏳ pending, ❓ not known. No faces and no hands (👍 is Mummy's; the folded hands wait on the owner), no stickers.

VERSIONS: she never sends a correction; she resends the whole list with 'revised' after the day ('Wedding list, Thu, revised'). This replaces 'Wedding list 23, 24', so the header carries no figure. On screen, one message card at a time.
THE THANK-YOU IN TYPE: from Friday her lists to you drop the closing 'Correct?' line. Nobody else's list ever does.
TIMING: lists go out at eleven at night, after her shift and dinner; in the day she replies within the minute; if 'Correct?' has no answer, she rings.
VOICE NOTES: never sends one ('you cannot tick a voice note'); when one comes, such as Mausi's long ones, she replies with a summary list of it ending on 'Correct?'.
FORWARDS: none, ever. Her one reply to a forward: a single ✅ under Papa's good-morning flower, every morning, the only reply he gets.
CALLS: Nani is rung, never texted, every evening since May for the BP; vendors are rung first and then sent a list of what was agreed, ending 'Thank you'.
FIGURES: the monthly BP log she sends Nani's doctor is the one thing she types with figures in it, and it stays off screen.
TYPOS: none; she rereads every list before sending; autocorrect on.

ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' or 'edited' label, no group chat on screen (owner, 23 Oct). The Sunday list to you is the one worth showing, early in chapter 5 if the writers have room, because it is where the player first sees the line with no status.

RULE 66 ON LINES TO YOU: every Hindi line to you is a command, a subjunctive ask, a verbless status or a possessive that agrees with the thing; none has you as the doer. ALL THREE MODES WITHIN THE CAP: every bubble here is at most 10 counted words (names and kinship names not counted, rule 62), checked by script; the two longer runs (5.03 and the temper line) are two bubbles each. No religious word, no caste word (रसोइया, never हलवाई), no brand, British spelling, no em or en dashes.

voices.name: You (the player, a voice only)

voice.register: Short, calm and level: the steadiest voice in a loud house, and the only one that puts a name on every line. ONE SHAPE, YOURS ALONE: one beat (a polite command, a bare noun, or 'Pehle ___'), with the listener's name on it. In Hinglish and Hindi the name opens the bubble, after it a comma ('Mami, dikhaiye.' | 'मामी, दिखाइए।'); in English it closes the bubble ('Let's see, Mami.'). The one opener that comes before the name is your exclamation ('Badhiya. Papa, aapke liye phone.'). Two to six words a bubble, at most two short sentences, never past seven words and always inside rule 62's ten. A bigger job never makes a longer bubble; it waits for the next exchange. Full stops, not exclamation marks: 'Badhiya.' is said flat, and the year's one '!' is 'Ek-ek karke!' in December. Questions are short and closed and ask for facts, never feelings ('Nani, dard?'). You speak last in an exchange, never open a scene, never speak between a decision's question and its pick, and sit in an outcome beat only as its fixed reply (rules 38 and 42). HOW THIS SHORT VOICE DIFFERS FROM THE OTHER SHORT ONES: Nani's closed fragments carry no name and send 'koi' to do the job; Mausa ji drops the subject and then does the job himself; Captain sahab gives the call, then one reason; Tinku ends on a score and 'haan?'; Mami reads your words back and asks 'Correct?'. You alone name the listener, every time. WHEN CROSS: you stay polite (your politeness never rises or falls, unlike Mummy's), but the name stands alone at the front, closed with a full stop, in every mode, and 'Pehle' names whoever was left waiting or left off ('Mama ji. Pehle Nani se miliye.' | 'Mama ji. See Nani first.'). Your anger is on someone else's behalf, never at a person. Once a year the noise beats you: 'Ek-ek karke!' BUDGET (proposal, kept from the cast file): three to six `you` bubbles a chapter, at most one a scene, the same whatever the player will pick (rule 38).
voice.mix: You mirror the listener, because being understood by each of them is your job, and that mirror is where your words come from. With Nani: plain everyday Hindi, no English beyond her own nouns (doctor, BP, ward, ticket, cake). With Mummy: her shop nouns (shutter, stock, bill, slip) on a Hindi frame, but never her English verb plus kar or ho ('check karo' is hers alone): you use the Hindi verb or none ('Mummy, shutter ki chaabi dijiye.'). With Papa: careful Hindi with his railway English (PNR, coach, berth) and his 'Reached', which stays in English letters in every mode. With Mama ji: English phrases, the most English you speak to an elder, and his own 'sorted' handed back ('Mama ji, sorted.'). With Tinku: young Hinglish, तुम and -ओ commands, her scorebook nouns (score, run, scorer). With Mausi, Mausa ji, Masterji, Captain sahab and Mami: polite Hinglish with -इए, using their own nouns only when you hand one back. Your base, when nobody sets it: Hinglish on a Hindi frame with English nouns, the shape of the younger speakers in the Dehradun study (realism notes [1]), bent back towards Hindi by a small-town home. What your English carries: the listener's words, nothing of your own. In Devanagari 'sorted' and 'set' are both 'सेट' (India review), never तय, which means 'decided'. Hindi mode lines are rebuilt from shapes that mark no gender (rule 66: commands, offers in the subjunctive, ने pasts that agree with the thing, verbless lines), never translated word for word. Numbers: none in speech in any mode. In a message, digits, and only when the fact is a number (ward 3, bed 12, berth 36, 2 days off).
tics: The name on every line. Hinglish and Hindi: the name first, then a comma ('Mausa ji, shukriya.' | 'मौसा जी, शुक्रिया।'). English: the name last ('Thanks, Mausa ji.'). Name first in Hindi also keeps rule 66's third check quiet, since नानी, मौसी, मामी and मौसा जी end in -ी. The only lines without a name are to someone the scene leaves unnamed (a child at the table, a cousin on the phone) and to a group, which you call 'sab' | 'सब' | 'everyone'. You never speak to the room otherwise.

You ask to see before anything: 'Dikhaiye.' In every chapter your first line at the hand-over is 'Let's see' with the giver's name. To Tinku and to children it is 'Dikhao', the one place your respect form drops, and readers hear the sibling.

Someone else first: 'Pehle ___' is yours alone in the cast (matrix 2.15; Masterji, Mami and Mausi's courtesy have dropped it). 'Masterji, pehle chai.' | 'Tea first, Masterji.' One thing first, then at most 'phir' and one more ('Tinku, pehle score. Phir chai.'); you never count on to a second or third, so no ordinal ever enters (Mami's old ordinals belong to nobody now).

One word for a whole job: 'Sab set.' | 'सब सेट।' | 'All set.', said to the person the job was for ('Nani, sab set.'). Never item by item: Mami itemises ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.') and you total.

Asked about yourself, you answer with the same two words you close a job with, 'Sab set.', and let the asker move on. The switchboard files itself as a job. It is not a dodge: never turned back on the asker ('You first, Mausi.' was Tinku's move in another form), never a figure (Mummy's, Papa's and Tinku's old dodges, C10), never somebody else's news.

You hand people their own words back, and only to their owner, with the owner's name in the same bubble, at most one line in three: Papa's 'Reached', Mama ji's 'sorted', Tinku's 'run tumhara' and 'score', Masterji's 'naap', Mummy's 'stock' and 'shutter', Captain sahab's 'toss', Nani's 'sach-sach'. Never a figure, never a judging note's words (rules 36 and 38), and never Mami's or Mausi's words, so the two chapters where you work beside them never blur.

No 'I', 'me', 'my' or 'please' in English and no मैं in Hindi, except in an offer in the subjunctive ('Torch main laaun?' | 'टॉर्च मैं लाऊँ?') and the album's one line, so nearly every line of yours can go on the button if the owner says yes to rulebook Q8.
Short closed questions for facts, never for feelings: 'Nani, dard?', 'Mausa ji, dawai ka time yaad hai?'. Never two question marks (Mausi's typed '??').
catchphrases: 'Dikhaiye.' | 'दिखाइए।' | 'Let's see.' (to Tinku and children: 'Dikhao.' | 'दिखाओ।'). The year's refrain, said to each person who hands you the work. Rule 66: the polite command the rule itself names (लिस्ट दिखाइए).

habits: Your phone: a plain smartphone in a plain charcoal-grey case, no sticker or charm, painted only in the present day lying face up on the bedside table, its screen a pale blank glow, every word live text (1.01; rule 30). Never in a hand, never an app's look, an app name, a maker's shape or a 'forwarded' label (rule 3). In a world chapter your messages appear as a plain message card under the panel (rule 40).

You always pick up and never leave a message unanswered; that is why everyone calls you. The story never says when, from where or how fast you answer, so a player on night shifts or an early bus fits (India review). You never write first about yourself.

You mirror each recipient's script and punctuation: a voice note to Nani; Mummy's own lowercase with no full stops; Papa's full stops and one fact a line, so he never reads you as cross; English to Mama ji, one message where he sends five; Tinku's lowercase; sentence case to the chapter voices.

What stays yours whatever the recipient: one message, never a burst; the recipient's name opens it in every mode, then a comma (a message is addressed like a letter, unlike your speech, where English puts the name last), except when the first word is their own word handed back or the greeting ('Reached, Papa.', 'Good morning, Papa.'), and the family group gets no name; Tinku's typed names stand alone on their own line, yours carry a comma; no line about yourself; never all capitals (realism notes [9]); never '??' (Mausi's); never a numbered list, a tick or a 'thing, status' item line (Mami's); never 'done' (Mami's), 'haan ji' (Mummy's typed tell) or 'ok' (Tinku's holding reply, Mausa ji's 'Ok.').

Your closer: 'sab set' with a thumbs-up, the one emoji you send. Ownership is free: Mummy's, Mausa ji's and Tinku's revised files each give the thumbs-up away, so it becomes yours (default yellow, no skin tone). No other emoji: the plain smiles are Mausi's (😊) and Tinku's (🙂); no person, skin-tone hand, coloured heart or folded hands (realism notes 3.2; rule 3). No stickers. In these samples the emoji is written as 👍.

English participles with no kar or ho, because they mark no gender and are not Mummy's verb frame: 'Reached' (to Papa only, his word, in English letters in every mode), 'Booked', 'Sorted' (to Mama ji only). In Hindi mode the rest is rebuilt from ने pasts that agree with the thing (बिल भेज दिया) or no verb, never पहुँच गया/गई.
Digits only when the fact is a number (ward, bed, berth, days off, the head-count of 14); no prices, no scores, no clock times except when Papa asks for one.
Voice notes: you send them only to Nani, who speaks to her phone rather than typing. Mausi's long voice notes get one typed line back.
